I don't get that John.  Survival curves are OK for individuals even
though we observe only binary outcomes.  Survival curves are properties
of both individuals and groups; the latter can be considered an average
of many of the former.  On a different note, we often compute
the estimated probability that each person lives to the actual time
she expired, given the covariates.  This is used in Cox-Snell residuals
for global (and not always powerful) goodness of fit checking.  -Frank
Harrell

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 1 May 2000, Amy K. Ferketich wrote:

> 
> I am using S+2000 and I would like to know how I can estimate
> a survival curve for each individual in my data set.  The outcome
> is time to drop-out, and I have fit a Cox regression model using
> several predictors.  Now, I would like to estimate a survival curve
> for each individual in the study so that I can determine the probability
> of survival at each time point (there are only 7 possible time points).  
> Thanks in advance.

What you  can do is to estimate the survivor function for an 
individual with a specific set of values of the predictors, x, thru the
relation

    S(t; x) = S_0(t)^exp(x * b).

S_0(t) == S(t; (0, ..., 0)) is the "baseline survivor function", which you
get an estimate of, and b is the vector of parameter estimates. 

Göran

messages.subject: [S] many files, several functions
messages.body_plain:
Hello fellow Splus users,

I have many ascii files, exported from arc/info grids, that I want to
analyze in Splus.  I have scanned in the files, and first need to change
the arc nodata (-9999) to NA, so I wrote this function:

arc.nodata<- function(x)
{
   n <-length(x)
   for (i in 1:n) {
     if (x[i] == -9999) x[i]<-NA
   }
   return(x)
}

Is there a more efficient way to do this than creating a script file
   calling this function once for each data file?

For the other functions I want to apply, should I create a list and loop
   through it?--something like:

for(i in 1:n){
   my.function(datalist[[i]])
}

I have heard that 'for' loops are inefficient, but I would have a long
   script file  as the alternative.  Of course, I already have a long
   script file to create the list!

Thank you for any suggestions.

Sandy
(novice function writer)

messages.subject: [S] Survival analysis, testing, interval censoring
messages.body_plain:
I have been asked for advice on a topic about which I have little 
training or experience (dangerous, I know!).

The experimenter planted groups of seeds under various discrete 
conditions. They were inspected weekly for survival (more 
specifically, did a predator come and eat them). For example, a 
particular seed was still present on day 14 but had disappeared by 
day 21. Some were gone at the first inspection (day 7), and some were 
still present when the experiment ceased on day 42. In other words, 
the survival times are mostly interval censored, some are right 
censored, and some are left censored. None are exact.

The experimenter wants to know if the different conditions affect survival.

I have been reading various books, including the Splus Guide to 
Statistics, V&R Ed. 3, Survival Analysis by Klein & Moeschberger 
(1997), Stat. Methods for Reliability Data by Meeker & Escobar 
(1998), and something of a picture is beginning to emerge.

After some exploring, it appears to me that:

  survfit() and survdiff() perform non-parametric fitting and testing 
between groups, but for right censored data only.

  kaplanMeier() fits non-parametric models to interval censored data, 
but I can find no Splus function for testing analagous to survfit().

  censorReg() fits parametric models, and anova() on a fitted object 
provides tests, but I think the experimenter is going to be more 
comfortable with a non-parametric approach. Since the experiment went 
only 6 weeks, and there are no exact times in the data set, most of 
the plots from plot.censorReg() fail and there isn't much to go on 
for assessing the choice of distribution.

So my basic questions are these:

  Is it not valid to perform surfdiff-like tests for interval censored data?

  Is there a function to perform tests on an object returned returned 
by kaplanMeier() that I have failed to find?

  What about faking it by generating random death times within the 
intervals (I would bet that I could re-randomize many times without 
changing the outcome of the tests).

And of course, any general advice about pitfalls or approaches would 
be appreciated. (Today I noticed V&R's warning that survdiff() tests 
of difference between groups are often used inappropriately.)

Thanks
-Don

--------------------------------
Don MacQueen
Environmental Protection Dept.
Livermore, CA, USA
Lawrence Livermore National Lab
--------------------------------

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 1 May 2000, Don MacQueen wrote:

> 
> I have been asked for advice on a topic about which I have little 
> training or experience (dangerous, I know!).
> 
> The experimenter planted groups of seeds under various discrete 
> conditions. They were inspected weekly for survival (more 
> specifically, did a predator come and eat them). For example, a 
> particular seed was still present on day 14 but had disappeared by 
> day 21. Some were gone at the first inspection (day 7), and some were 
> still present when the experiment ceased on day 42. In other words, 
> the survival times are mostly interval censored, some are right 
> censored, and some are left censored. None are exact.
> 
> The experimenter wants to know if the different conditions affect survival.
> 
> I have been reading various books, including the Splus Guide to 
> Statistics, V&R Ed. 3, Survival Analysis by Klein & Moeschberger 
> (1997), Stat. Methods for Reliability Data by Meeker & Escobar 
> (1998), and something of a picture is beginning to emerge.

I would suggest that you have discrete-time observations, and use the
methods appropriate to those rather than to continuous survival.  I think I
would use conditional logistic models (for being alive at week n
given that you were alive at week n-1).  This is an unusual topic in
survival books, but is widely used in demographic and actuarial work (as
they have annual censuses): I think Cox and Oakes' book discusses this.

Another area where these tests are widely (mis-)used is in oncology with
annual followup, and my wife and I wrote a paper on that which you can find
on my web site with a review of possible (non-linear, it fact) models.

messages.subject: Re: [S] individual survival curves
messages.body_plain:
In response to Amy Fekitich:

    fit <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x1 + ....., data= mydata)
    curves <- survfit(fit, newdata=mydata)
    
When survfit() is applied to a Cox model, one gets a predicted curve for each
row of 'newdata'.  If newdata is missing, the single survival curve for an
``average'' subject is returned.  
  It is also easy to look at individual curves: say subjects 21 and 22
        summary(curves[21:22])
        plot( curves[21:22])
        
Since I don't use the GUI I can't comment on which buttons, if any, to push in
order to duplicate the above.

        Terry Therneau

Department of Epidemiology and Community Medicine of the University of
Ottawa and the Loeb Health Research Institute at The Ottawa Hospital

MULTIVARIATE DEPENDENCIES

Lecturers: David Cox, Nuffield College, Oxford and Nanny Wermuth, ZUMA -
Center for Survey Research, Mannheim

Registration Fee: $300.00 (Cdn) - The fee to Graduate Students is $150.00.
Includes the lecturer's book 
"Multivariate Dependencies - Models, Analysis and Interpretation", Chapman
and Hall, 1996

The aim of the workshop:

The workshop will provide a systematic discussion of a basis for the
analysis and interpretation of complex multivariate data. The workshop is
designed for those making extensive use of statistical methods in health and
social science research who need to meaningfully interact with both other
statisticians and scientists / decision makers. Common issues and themes
that arise in almost any form of careful data analysis, complex or
otherwise, will be discussed. 

The workshop is intended for those concerned with the analysis and
interpretation of complex data, especially but not entirely observational
data. The applications from the social and health sciences are wide-ranging
including, for example, studies of medical interventions and of sociological
or psychological development. While the primary emphasis will be on
statistical methods for direct use in applications, some issues of
theoretical interest will also be addressed. One central theme will be the
role of independence graphs and on processes by which the data could have
been generated. This theme suggests the recasting and restructuring of
fairly standard and well known statistical techniques to better focus and
report on important data analysis issues. 

No software presentations will be given, the emphasis being largely on
methods which can be implemented within standard packages. A fairly similar
workshop was given last Fall at the Fields Institute in Toronto
(http://www.fields.utoronto.ca/cis-scourse.html#MARKOV). 

While the workshop is based in part on the lecturers' book "Multivariate
Dependencies - Models, Analysis and Interpretation" (Chapman and Hall,
1996), a number of important developments since the book will be described.
As well as core material a number of specific research questions will be
discussed in detail; the corresponding data can be obtained via the internet
(soon at http://www.lri.ca/).

contact information (phone, fax, email and surface mail address) so that

student status" you will be presenting when you arrive.

Official receipt will be for attendance at a workshop at the University of
Ottawa. We are planning on having the text "Multivariate Dependencies -
Models, Analysis and Interpretation", Chapman and Hall, 1996 available for
handout at the workshop.  

For further information the course organizer, Keith O'Rourke at
multdep at lri.ca.

messages.subject: [S] Summary for S.D. of geometric means
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary for S.D. of geometric means
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Frank E Harrell Jr and Dave Parkhurst who responded to my previous
question. Both are very helpful. Frank suggested to calculate
S.E. of Geometric means using Bootstrap(). Dave's comments is below.

.............
One common approach is to report the so-called geometric SD, which is just
exp(SD.y), where SD.y is the std. dev. of the logs.  That, of course, does
NOT estimate the SD of the original data.  It only allows you to reconstruct
the normal distn. that the logs are supposed to have.

A major reference on log-normal distributions is Aitchison, J. and J. A. C.
Brown (1957). The Lognormal Distribution with special reference to its uses
in economics. Cambridge, U.K., Cambridge University Press.

Depending on what you are using geometric means for, you might consider the
warnings against their use in my paper, Parkhurst, D. F. (1998). "Arithmetic
versus geometric means for environmental concentration data." Environmental
Science and Technology 32(3): 92A-98A.
..............

Ming

messages.subject: [S] Summary: many files, several functions
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for all the helpful replies to my questions! (Patrick Connolly,
Jeff Johnston, Bill Dunlap, Greg Snow, Bill Venables, Manuela Huso, Peter
Alspach, Alan Gross, Brian Ripley, Gerald Jean, Bill Munger) Below is a
summary of answers.
Sandy

For changing ?9999 to NA:

1. No looping is necessary to replace ?9999 with NA because of the vector
properties.
     x[x==-9999] <- NA

2. An alternate method was suggested, using read.table, in which you can
specify na.string as the "-9999" value while reading in the data at the
same time.

3. If the data are in a list, this option was suggested:
new.list <- lapply(old.list, FUN = function(x) x[x == -9999] <- NA)

With regard to long script files:

1. Use a text editor, such as emacs or sed.  You can also use 'For' to
write and execute a long script (Unix and Splus 2000).

About the use of 'for' loops, and how to apply a function to many data
objects:

1. If you use a loop to call the function for a list, you need to store the
results:
for(i in 1:n){
     datalist[[i] <- my.function(datalist[[i]])
  }

2. for lists and data frames you can use either lapply or sapply:
output<-lapply(datalist, my.function, extra, args, to, my.function)
     (sapply runs lapply then "simplifies" the output)

3. There is a trade off in using 'for' loops.  They can be inefficient but
you may waste more time figuring out an alternative than you will save in
the long run (depending on the length of the loop).

4. Looping through a list (as I had written in my question) is not
recommended, but the alternate solution would depend on my objectives and
set up.

5. These were suggested solutions:

for(i in seq(along=datalist)) datalist[[i]] <- my.function(datalist[[i]])
or
datalist <- lapply(datalist, my.function)

6. At the top level (not inside a function), 'for' loops are not much of a
problem, but lapply is usually preferred.

**************************************************************************************
On Mon, 1 May 2000 sandy_haire at usgs.gov wrote:

Hello fellow Splus users,

I have many ascii files, exported from arc/info grids, that I want to
analyze in Splus.  I have scanned in the files, and first need to change
the arc nodata (-9999) to NA, so I wrote this function:

arc.nodata<- function(x)
{
   n <-length(x)
   for (i in 1:n) {
     if (x[i] == -9999) x[i]<-NA
   }
   return(x)
}

Is there a more efficient way to do this than creating a script file
   calling this function once for each data file?

For the other functions I want to apply, should I create a list and loop
   through it?--something like:

for(i in 1:n){
   my.function(datalist[[i]])
}

I have heard that 'for' loops are inefficient, but I would have a long
   script file  as the alternative.  Of course, I already have a long
   script file to create the list!

Thank you for any suggestions.

Sandy
(novice function writer)

messages.subject: [S] exact ci for a proportion: summary
messages.subject_clean: [S] exact ci for a proportion: summary
messages.body_plain:
Thanks very much to everyone who replied --I had several excellent answers (summarized below) all of which seem to get the job done, with some variation in the input options (some allow you to specify the width of the ci explicitly), i tried three which all worked equally well and produced the same answers. -original question- Hello, Does anyone know if is there function in S+ to calculate exact confidence intervals for proportions based on binomial probability distribution (e.g. k successes in n trials). Are the confidence intervals reported by prop.test exact? Thanks much in advance. Tim ____________________________________________________________________________ __________ Try this: binom.conf<-function(r,n){ #95% exact binom conf int from Armitage and Berry '94 (pg 121) #if (r==0) lower<-0 lower<-ifelse(r==0,0,r/(r+(n-r+1)*qf(.975,(2*(n-r+1)),(2*r)))) #if (r==n) upper<-1 upper<-ifelse(r==n,1,(r+1)/(r+1+(n-r)/qf(.975,(2*(r+1)),(2*(n-r))))) return(list(lower=lower,upper=upper))} _____________________________________ exact.binom.CI <- function(P, N, k) { # Exact Binomial Condfidence limits. ; # To get 95% limits, enter (0.95, trials, successes); # Ref: Clopper & Pearson, Biometrika (1934), v26, p.404 ; if(N > k & k >= 1) return(c(pl = qbeta((1 - P)/2, k, N - k + 1), pu = qbeta(1 - (1 - P)/ 2, k + 1, N - k))) if(N > 0 & N == k) return(c(pl = P^(1/n), pu = 1)) if(N > 0 & k == 0) return(c(pl = 0, pu = (1 - P^(1/N)))) ______________________________________ binomCI function(n, k, alpha1 = 0.05, alpha2 = 0.05) { #This function finds Confidence Intervals (L, U) on a binomi al #parameter p, so that P(L <= p) >= 1 - alpha1, # and P(p <= U) >= 1 - alpha2 nu1 <- 2 * (n + 1 - k) nu2 <- 2 * k if(k == 0) p1 <- 0 else p1 <- 1/(1 + (nu1/nu2) * qf(1 - alpha1, nu1, nu2)) nu1 <- 2 * (k + 1) nu2 <- 2 * (n - k) if(k == n) p2 <- 1 else p2 <- (W <- (nu1/nu2) * qf(1 - alpha2, nu1, nu2))/(1 + W) c(p1, p2) } ______________________________ The Hmisc library has the binconf function which computes the exact CL and the less conservative Wilson interval. See http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/s/Hmisc.html - the entry under Online Help Documentation. ____________________________ Collett, D. Modeling Binary Data, London: Chapman & Hall (1991), pp 23-25. It is also referenced as the source for a SAS macro EXACTPCI, V1.2 > binom.conf function(y, n, alpha = 0.05) { if(y == 0) lower <- 0 else lower <- y/(y + (n - y + 1) * qf(1 - (alpha/2), 2 * (n - y + 1), 2 * y)) if(y == n) upper <- 1 else upper <- (y + 1)/(y + 1 + (n - y)/qf(1 - (alpha/2), 2 * (y + 1), 2 * (n - y))) cbind(lower, upper) } _________________________________________ Here is a local file (created by Terry Therneau) that will give you exact CI, plus the associated helpfiles (for 3.4 and 5.1 formats). Let me know if you have any questions. ~> X-Sender: tjwade at uclink4.berkeley.edu (Unverified) ~> Date: Wed, 03 May 2000 11:43:37 -0700 ~> To: s-news at wubios.wustl.edu ~> From: "Timothy J. Wade" ~> Subject: [S] exact confidence interval for proportion ~> Mime-Version: 1.0 ~> X-loop: s-news ~> ~> ~> Hello, ~> ~> Does anyone know if is there function in S+ to calculate exact confidence ~> intervals for proportions based on binomial probability distribution (e.g. ~> k successes in n trials). Are the confidence intervals reported by ~> prop.test exact? ~> ~> Thanks much in advance. ~> ~> Tim ~> ~> ~> Timothy J. Wade ~> Doctoral Candidate ~> UC Berkeley School of Public Health ~> Department of Epidemiology ~> Berkeley, CA ~> ~> 510-548-9883 (phone) ~> 510-548-9876 (fax) # # Exact binomial confidence limits # Based on equation 10.7 of Feller volume 1 # The other approximations make use of the continuity correction cibinom <- function(k, n, p=.95, method=c('exact', 'arcsin', 'normal', 'anscombe')) { nn <- max(length(k), length(n), length(p)) if (nn>1) { k <- rep(k, length=nn) n <- rep(n, length=nn) p <- rep(p, length=nn) } p2 <- (1-p)/2 method <- match.arg(method) if (method=='exact') { dummy1 <- ifelse(k==0, 1, k) #avoid an error message of qbeta dummy2 <- ifelse(k==n, n-1, k) upper <- ifelse(k==n, 1, 1- qbeta(p2, n-dummy2, k+1)) lower <- ifelse(k==0, 0, 1- qbeta(1-p2, n+1-k, dummy1)) } else if (method=='normal'){ #normal approx, poorest pp <- k/n std <- sqrt(pp * (1-pp) /n) upper <- pp + .5/n - qnorm(p2)*std lower <- pp + qnorm(p2)*std - .5/n } else if (method=='arcsin'){ # use the arcsin transform ap <- asin(sqrt(k/n)) ap1<- asin(sqrt(ifelse(k==n, k, k+.5)/n)) ap2<- asin(sqrt(ifelse(k==0, k, k-.5)/n)) std<- sqrt(.25/n) upper <- (sin(ap1 - qnorm(p2)*std))^2 lower <- (sin(ap2 + qnorm(p2)*std))^2 } else if (method=='anscombe'){ # anscombe's method con <- 3/8 ap <- asin(sqrt((k+con)/(n + 2*con))) ap1<- asin(sqrt((con+ifelse(k==n, k, k+.5))/(n + 2*con))) ap2<- asin(sqrt((con+ifelse(k==0, k, k-.5))/(n + 2*con))) std<- sqrt(.25/(n+.5)) upper <- ((sin(ap1 - qnorm(p2)*std))^2) lower <- ((sin(ap2 + qnorm(p2)*std))^2) } else stop("Invalid method") if (nn==1) c(lower=lower, upper=upper) else cbind(lower=lower, upper=upper) } Content-Type: TEXT/plain; name="cibinom.d"; charset=us-ascii; x-unix-mode=0644 Content-Description: cibinom.d Content-MD5: rMkUcdo8MtWdK6Drs3VLnQ== .BG .FN cibinom .TL Confidence limits for the binomial .DN Give exact confidence limits for a binomial parameter .CS cibinom(k, n, p=0.95, method=c("exact", "arcsin", "normal", "anscombe")) .RA .AG k number of successes .AG n number of trials .OA .AG p probability level for the (two-sided) interval .AG method the method of approximation. The approximate methods are supplied for comparison purposes. .RT Either a vector containing the lower and upper limits, or a two column matrix of lower and upper limits. .DT The exact method is based on equation 10.7 of Feller, which relates binomial probabilities to tail area of the beta distribution. The arcsin method is based on the approximation that asin(sqrt(p)) is approximately normal with a variance of .25/n. The Anscombe approximation is a refinement of the arcsin method. The normal or Gaussian approximation assumes that p is normal with variance p(1-p)/n. It is known to be poor. The arcsin, Anscombe, and normal approximations incorporate a continuity correction. .SH REFERENCES W.F. Feller (1950). An Introduction to Probability Theory and its Applications, Volume 1, Chapter 6, Wiley. .br F.J. Anscombe (1949). Transformations of Poisson, binomial and negative-binomial data. wih Scott Emerson and John Kittleson

June 13-14              Royal Society of Medicine, London, UK

June 20-21              Basel, Switzerland

June 26-27              Paris, France

June 29-30              Heidelberg, Germany

Course Description
Increasingly, clinical trials are conducted using group sequential methods
in order to address the ethical and efficiency issues that arise when
performing experiments with human volunteers. The design, conduct, and
analysis of a sequential clinical trial is necessarily more involved than
that for a clinical trial in which the data would only be analyzed at the
end of the study. In this short course we present the additional issues that
must be considered when conducting a group sequential trial. The group
sequential methods are illustrated using S+SeqTrial , a module for the
design, monitoring, and analysis of clinical trials. Course participants
will receive hands-on instruction in the use of S+SeqTrial to perform the
various statistical tasks necessary from start to finish in the conduct of a
clinical trial.

messages.body_plain:
I'm using Splus2000 on Windows98.

I'm trying to plot a groupedData object and am having a bit of problem
getting it into the shape that I'd like.  Our data are from a clinical trial
with therapists nested within treatments like the following:

Treatment A    Treatment B
Therapist 1      Therapist 4
Therapist 2      Therapist 5
Therapist 3      Therapist 6

Each subject receives one treatment from a single therapist.  We have a
dependent measure from each session (up to 24 sessions).  Here is my
groupedData command:

df.psych <- groupedData(dv ~ session | subject, data=df.psych,
outer= ~treatment/therapist, labels = list(x="Session No.",
y="Total DV score"))

I would like to plot the data with one cell/graph per therapist/treatment
combination, such as:

TxA/Th1        TxB/Th4

TxA/Th2        TxB/Th5

TxA/Th3        TxB/Th6

However, I haven't been able to get that format yet.

plot(df.psych, outer= ~therapist) gives me a single column of therapist
graphs (which makes sense to me)

plot(dr.psych, outer= ~treatment/therapist) gives me a 6 x 2 matrix of
graphs with 6 empty graphs because therapists only provide one type of
treatment.

Any suggestions about how to get the 3 x 2 matrix of graphs?

Thank you,

Dave Atkins        datkins at u.washington.edu

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Survival analysis, testing, interval censoring
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Survival analysis, testing, interval censoring
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Frank Harrell, Brian Ripley, Gerrit Eichner, Terry 
Therneau, and Anne York for your suggestions. Excerpts from their 
responses are:

-- Frank Harrell --
If the survival times are heavily tied (i.e., only 6 possible values as
assessments are only made weekly) you might consider an
ordinal logistic regression model as this model expects tied data
and a full survival model would not gain much precision in this
case..

-- Brian Ripley --
I would suggest that you have discrete-time observations, and use the
methods appropriate to those rather than to continuous survival.  I think I
would use conditional logistic models (for being alive at week n
given that you were alive at week n-1).  This is an unusual topic in
survival books, but is widely used in demographic and actuarial work (as
they have annual censuses): I think Cox and Oakes' book discusses this.

-- Gerrit Eichner --
You may want to take a look at Jon A. Wellner's (Univ. of Washington)
pages, especially at
http://www.stat.washington.edu/jaw/RESEARCH/SOFTWARE/software.list.html
and there at Readme under "Interval Censoring"

or at Piet Groeneboom's (Technical Univ. of Delft) page
http://ssor.twi.tudelft.nl/~pietg

and there at Interval Censoring (...) under "Software development for
Statistical Inverse Problems".

-- Terry Therneau --
 My advice: use survreg or censorReg
 As long as there are not outliers (and obviously there are not), then a
 Gaussian distribution assumption is essentially a comparison of means, and
 it will be fine.

-- Anne York --
You might consider some of the mark-recapture methods. These are
multinomial models with constraints. Your situation seems
simpler than most animal studies, if the seeds really don't move unless the
predator removes them. The resight probabilities and the survival rates can
be jointly estimated. If the resight rates are high,  it will be easy to
estimate the survival rates between the weeks (depending on sample size).

There is a nice program called mark, freely available for estimating the
parameters in these models on Gary White's website:

http://www.cnr.colostate.edu/~gwhite/software.html

There is documentation available on his web site, but  a nice tutorial for
the program is available on Evan Cooch's web site:

http://canuck.dnr.cornell.edu

- Don

--- the original query ---
> I have been asked for advice on a topic about which I have little
> training or experience (dangerous, I know!).
>
> The experimenter planted groups of seeds under various discrete
> conditions. They were inspected weekly for survival (more
> specifically, did a predator come and eat them). For example, a
> particular seed was still present on day 14 but had disappeared by
> day 21. Some were gone at the first inspection (day 7), and some were
> still present when the experiment ceased on day 42. In other words,
> the survival times are mostly interval censored, some are right
> censored, and some are left censored. None are exact.
>
> The experimenter wants to know if the different conditions affect survival.
>
>
>
> I have been reading various books, including the Splus Guide to
> Statistics, V&R Ed. 3, Survival Analysis by Klein & Moeschberger
> (1997), Stat. Methods for Reliability Data by Meeker & Escobar
> (1998), and something of a picture is beginning to emerge.
>
> After some exploring, it appears to me that:
>
>
>
>    survfit() and survdiff() perform non-parametric fitting and testing
> between groups, but for right censored data only.
>
>    kaplanMeier() fits non-parametric models to interval censored data,
> but I can find no Splus function for testing analagous to survfit().
>
>    censorReg() fits parametric models, and anova() on a fitted object
> provides tests, but I think the experimenter is going to be more
> comfortable with a non-parametric approach. Since the experiment went
> only 6 weeks, and there are no exact times in the data set, most of
> the plots from plot.censorReg() fail and there isn't much to go on
> for assessing the choice of distribution.
>
> So my basic questions are these:
>
>
>
>    Is it not valid to perform surfdiff-like tests for interval censored data?
>
>
>
>    Is there a function to perform tests on an object returned returned
> by kaplanMeier() that I have failed to find?
>
>    What about faking it by generating random death times within the
> intervals (I would bet that I could re-randomize many times without
> changing the outcome of the tests).
>
> And of course, any general advice about pitfalls or approaches would
> be appreciated. (Today I noticed V&R's warning that survdiff() tests
> of difference between groups are often used inappropriately.)
>
> Thanks
> -Don
--------------------------------
Don MacQueen
Environmental Protection Dept.
Livermore, CA, USA
Lawrence Livermore National Lab
--------------------------------

messages.subject: [S] (summary) CI for GAM by boostrapping
messages.body_plain:
Dear S community,

Three days ago I asked for advice on bootstrapping GAMs to obtain 
confidence intervals.  Thank you to those you responded.
Here is an edited version of the replies I got:

>>From Prof. Ripley:
I think you first need to decide what to bootstrap. For regression
models it is usual to bootstrap residuals, not data points.  I would
take a look at library(boot) (on statlib), which has extensive
examples of bootstrapping glms that you could adapt.  (The book it
goes with, Davison & Hinkley, is very highly recommended (by me) too.)

>>From Eusebio Arenal Gutiérrez:
See the S-library of Davison and Hinkley book.
Davison, A.C. and Hinkley, D.V. (1997). Bootstrap Methods and Their
Application. Cambridge University Press.  There is a chapter about 
bootstrap on glm and gam models

>>From Vito Muggeo:
If you are interested in bootstrapping coefficients in glm() model you can
type:

a<-bootstrap(data.frame,coef(glm(...)),B=1000,trace=F)
summary(a) 

and you get the confidence intervals (empirical and BCa) for the 
coefficients.  I used it for coef(glm(...)) and seems to work. It should work 
for fitted.values(gam(...)) too.
-----------------
Unfortunately our library has lost Davison and Hinkley's book!  By the time 
the one I ordered from another library arrives, I will have had to bind my 
thesis if I want to make it to the graduation next weekend.  I have tried 
Prof. Ripley's suggestion of bootstrapping the residuals and typed in:

trial <- bootstrap(mydata, resid(eval(mygam$call))
and when I ask for the summary, I receive at the end this message:

  z0 is outside range (-.25, .25), this indicates extreme bias,
assumptions underlying BCa interval may be violated in: limits.bca(object, 
probs, frame.eval.jack = frame.eval.jack)

I must be doing something wrong.  Can someone advise?  My goal is to 
get 90% confidence intervals for my GAMs and plot them instead of the 
2se curves in the gam plots.  I use S-Plus 4.5, Professional edition, on 
Win95.

Thank you,

> for fitted.values(gam(...)) too.
> -----------------
> Unfortunately our library has lost Davison and Hinkley's book!  By the time 
> the one I ordered from another library arrives, I will have had to bind my 
> thesis if I want to make it to the graduation next weekend.  I have tried 
> Prof. Ripley's suggestion of bootstrapping the residuals and typed in:
> 
> trial <- bootstrap(mydata, resid(eval(mygam$call))

Oops. That is not how you bootstrap residuals: you need to generate new
y's by adding them back to the predictions.  Here's an example from
V&R3:

library(boot)
fit <- lm(calls ~ year, data=phones)
ph <- data.frame(phones, res=resid(fit), fitted=fitted(fit))
ph.fun <- function(data, i) {
  d <- data
  d$calls <- d$fitted + d$res[i]
  coef(update(fit, data=d))
}
ph.lm.boot <- boot(ph, ph.fun, R=499)
ph.lm.boot

and there are many more in that library.

--

messages.subject: [S] Prediction intervals from lme
messages.body_plain:
Greetings all,

I'm trying to design a study to test whether or not loblolly pine in 
Uruguay tapers the same as grown in SE US.  Our brief is to see 
whether a model known as the Max-Burkhart equation with 
already-estimated parameters is adequate for these new populations. 
So, I believe that my null hypothesis will be that there *is* a 
difference, and the alternative will be that there is not.

The target population is as follows: there are 10 different stands, 
within each of which there are many many trees.  We will select and 
fell n2 trees from n1 stands and take n3 diameter and height 
measurements on each sample tree at different locations up the bole.

I'm presently interested in gauging the optimal relativesizes of n1, 
n2 and n3 based on criteria for model quality that are currently 
obscure.  I have some reconnaissance data from Uruguay and I'm trying 
to figure out how to use it to do a pre-hoc power study.  I have data 
for two stands of 10 and 17 trees, with 5-7 measurements on the bole 
for each tree.  I've fit a mixed-effects linear model on the 
measurement errors (differences between measurements at Uruguay and 
predicted using SE US function) as follows:

USerror[ijk] = b0 + beta[i] + beta[j/i] + b1*rel_height + 
b2*rel_height^2 + epsilon[ijk]

where USerror[ijk] is the difference between measurement and 
prediction for the kth location on the jth tree at the ith site, b0 
is the population intercept, beta[i] a random site intercept, 
beta[j/i] a random tree intercept nested within site, rel_height a 
fixed effect (0<rel_height<1), and the rest relatively obvious.  I'm 
happy with the model.  I fiddled with various other options and this 
one does just nicely.

The output provides estimates of standard deviations for the random 
site, tree-within-site, and within-tree terms.  (I am presently 
leaving aside within-tree residual correlation structure).  Now I'd 
like to place a prediction interval around the a prediction of 
USerror as a function of relative height.  To clarify: I'd like a 95% 
prediction interval for a randomly-located measurement on a 
randomly-selected tree within a randomly-selected site.   Hopefully 
this will be a function of the above standard deviations and the 
three hierarchical sample sizes n1, n2, n3.  I'd like to then examine 
the behaviour of these intervals as the sample sizes change.

Non Splus-related question (ignore if you wish!): is this credible as 
an approach to assist in design?

Splus-related question: I can't see prediction intervals in lme, and 
I haven't seen an answer to a question like this in the archives.  Is 
there one?  Ought I simply bootstrap, or are there other 
alternatives?  I'm running Splus 2000 on Win '95.

Non Splus-related question (ignore if you wish!): if I bootstrap, is 
here a good reference to guide me through multi-level bootstrapping? 
The UI library has the following references, if anyone could nominate 
a particularly strong book it would be welcomed.

Chernick, Michael		Bootstrap methods : a practitioner's 
guide	1999

Shao, Jun.		The jackknife and bootstrap			1995

Hjorth, J. S. Urban.	Computer intensive statistical methods : 
validat	1994

Efron, Bradley.		An introduction to the bootstrap		1993

Mooney, Christopher	Bootstrapping : a nonparametric approach to 
stat	1993

Hall, Peter		The bootstrap and Edgeworth expansion	1992

??			Exploring the limits of bootstrap		1992

Efron, Bradley.		The jackknife, the bootstrap, and other 
resampli	1982

Thankyou so much!

--
Andrew

messages.subject: Re: [S] Permutation of n Numbers
messages.body_plain:
Your problem is that you clobber one of the values in p as you are
swapping.  You should probably be using replace() just once with 

p <- replace(p, c(k, j), p[c(j, k)])

In fact, lets check:

> Permu
function(n)
{
        k <- n
        p <- 1:n
        repeat {
                u <- runif(1)
                j <- floor(k * u) + 1
                p <- replace(p, c(k, j), p[c(j, k)])
                k <- k - 1
                if(k < 1)
                        return(p)
        }
}
>
> Permu(5)
[1] 1 3 2 4 5
> Permu(5)
[1] 3 1 5 2 4
> Permu(5)
[1] 4 3 2 1 5

But the function is unnecessary since there is already a very quick one to
do the same job built-in:

> sample(5)
[1] 3 2 1 4 5

messages.subject: [S] lme for long.data
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus users,

I am attempting to fit a model for longitudinal
data with Splus's lme function. It does not give
me the output I expect; perhaps someone with 
more lme experience might have insights on this...

My dataset has m patients and ni observations for 
each patient. For each data point, y_ij at time
t_ij, I am trying to fit a random intercept for 
each patient, b_i, a term representing temporally 
correlated variability, v_ij, and measurement 
error term,e_ij.

y_ij = Mu + b_i + v_ij + e_ij

Mu is the overall intercept.
b_i is i.i.d N(0,sigma_b^2) 
e_ij's are i.i.d. N(0,sigma_eps^2)

each vector v_i has expectation (0,..,0) and 
covariance(v_i) uses the exponential semi-variogram
model (the continous analog of the first order
auto-regressive correlation model), i.e, the 
corr(v_ij,v_ik) = exp(eta* abs(t_ik - t_ij)).
The covariance matrix for (v_i) is multiplied
by the scalar sigma_v^2. Of course, the same 
eta and sigma_v^2 is fit across all patients. 

The terms I would like estimated are : 
(1) sigma_b^2, (2) sigma_v^2, (3) sigma_eps^2
(4) eta (parameter inside continous AR model).

mydata$id are patient id's
mydata$Y is the response
mydata$time are the t_ij's

I tried the following : 
lme(fixed=Y~1,random=~1,cluster=~id, serial.structure="ar1.continuous",
re.structure=c("identity"),serial.covariate=~time,data=mydata)

This only gives me 3 parameter estimates of interest
(2 variance components and the eta)! What should I
be fitting instead ?

Any tips would be really appreciated.

Thankyou very much.

Murali

messages.subject: [S] Summary: Controlling tick labels in trellis
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Controlling tick labels in trellis
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Stephen Smith and Francois Collin for the assist!

I asked the following:

I've checked the documentation, S-news archives and V&R to no avail... how
does one control the size, orientation etc of tick labels in Trellis
graphics?  Axis labels can be controlled via a list argument to xlab or
ylab, but I missed the analog or alternative for axes tick mark labels...

Stephen Smith noted:

These settings are part of the scale=list(...) argument in the trellis plot
command --- see trellis.args in the help file

Francois Collin gave some syntax:

Here's the syntax:
   dotplot(Group ~ Yvar | Cvar,
                xlab='Put this under the x-axis',
                scale = list(x = list(at = 1:10,
                                            labels=1:10)
                                )
             )

Rob Kronlund

messages.body_plain:
Does anyone know of how to separate the two pieces of the string "a & b"
into the two string "a" "b"?  "a & b" was created by

  combo <- paste(drug1, drug2, sep = " & ")

So, I'm looking for the "unpaste" function.  In SAS, I'd use

drug1 = SCAN(combo, 1, "&");
drug2 = scan(combo, 2, "&");

Any suggestions?  I'm *sure* I've done this in the past, but I've hit a
total mental block.  The hmisc function first.word looked like it would
do the job, but it's designed for pulling apart expressions, and I'm
pretty sure I haven't used that in the past.

Thanks for any suggestions, especially of the form "try ?func" ;).

Rob

P.S.  Some background, in case you're interested:

drug1 is the first therapy a patient is assigned; drug2 is the second
(which could be the same).

I then want to construct a table of frequencies along the lines of what
I would get from:

PROC TABULATE;
  CLASS DRUG1 DRUG2;
  TABLE DRUG1 * DRUG2;
RUN;

If I use table(drug1, drug2), I get pretty close, but I would like the
results to be more like

drug1  drug2  n  pct
a      a      .
a      b      .
b      b      .
b      a      .
c      none   .

I have also used paste, as in:

> combo <- paste(drug1, drug2, sep = " & ")
> table(combo)

and this comes very close, except that I can't sort things in quite the
right order (by drug1 and then by drug2 within drug1).  This is where
the "unpaste" or function would come in handy.  R.

----
Rob Balshaw, PhD                            Synectics Health Corporation

messages.subject: [S] minimization in Splus
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus Users,

I'm trying to implement a very simple example of indirect inference
in Splus but get problems with the minimization. The goal is to estimate
the unknown parameter theta of an MA(1) process (with fixed innovation
variance equal to 1) based on the parameter pi of an AR(1) auxiliary
representation. The parameter pi is estimated first on the original data,
yielding pihat, then on simulated data from the MA(1), yielding pistar,
a function of theta by construction. The indirect estimator of theta
is the value of theta that brings pistar as ``close'' as possible to pihat.

Here is my Splus code:

n=100
s=10
data_arima.sim(model=list(ma=0.5),n)
hatpi_ar.gm(data,order=1,iterh=0,iterb=0,effgm=0.9)$ar
inov_rnorm(n*s)
 obj.fct_function(starpi,dif){
 simu_arima.sim(model=list(ma=starpi),innov=inov)
 (dif-ar.gm(simu,order=1,iterh=0,iterb=0,effgm=0.9)$ar)^2
}
nlminb(start=0.5,objective=obj.fct,dif=hatpi)

ww_seq(-0.9,0.9,0.0113)
w_ww
for(i in 1:length(ww)){w[i]_obj.fct(ww[i],hatpi)}
plot(ww,w)

Note that the size of the simulated data is s*n and that it
is possible to use a robust (GM) estimator on the AR model.

The problem is that the minimization with ``nlminb'' doesn't
always work, even when there is a clear minimum in the objective
function around 0.5  (try to run the code several times).

Does anybody have an idea about why I get this problem with
the minimization? Am I not using the ``nlminb'' correctly?

Thanks in advance for help.

Marc Genton

messages.subject_clean: [S] Removing unused levels from multiple factors in a data.frame
messages.body_plain:
I have a data.frame of several thousand rows in the form of:
(The Product, component.1 and component.2 columns are factors)

> test
    Product   component.1   component.2   qty 
1       A          p1                  q1                 25
2       A          p2                  q1                 15
3       B          p1                  q1                 12
4       C          xa                  q1                   1
5       B          p4                  q2                   8
6       A          p1                  q2                 14
7       A          p2                  q1                   1

to which I apply various business rules to "clean" the data.  
For example in the above table component xa is invalid 
and that record needs to be removed using:

> test <- test[test$component.1 != "xa",]

> test
     Product   component.1   component.2   qty 
1       A          p1                   q1                25
2       A          p2                   q1                15
3       B          p1                   q1                12
5       B          p4                   q2                  8
6       A          p1                   q2                14
7       A          p2                   q1                  1

Although this appears to be correct, the missing levels are still present in 
all 
of the factors:

> levels(test$Product)
[1] "A" "B" "C"
> levels(test$component.1)
[1] "p1" "p2" "p4" "xa"

The only way I have been able to deal with these "extra" levels is to drop them 
on a column by column basis such as:
> test$Product <- test$Product[,drop=TRUE]
> test$component.1 <- test$component.1[,drop=TRUE]
> test$component.2 <- test$component.2[,drop=TRUE]

Is there a way to deal with the entire data frame and drop all unused levels in 
all
columns that are factors?

Thanks
Bruce Aldridge
SageTree, Inc.
bruce.e.aldridge at wdc.com
-------------------------------

messages.subject: [S] Assignment operator in S-Plus
messages.body_plain:
At the almost certain risk of being jumped on by many (or worse yet,
starting a long and unproductive debate), I ask why a syntax is
considered desirable in which

        x>-1

is a logical expression for a comparison and

        x<-1 

reassigns the value of x ?

I understand that C programmers are irritated by the use of the underscore,
which they typically see as part of a variable name rather than an operator.
On the other hand, in almost 15 years of using S I have not reconciled myself
to the use of the <- as a kluge for the unfortunate (?) loss of the arrow
symbol on the old APL keyboard.

        Alan Zaslavsky

freedom, indicating that my data are underdispersed.

Possibly.  It might just indicate that the distribution theory behind that
assumption is not satisfied. 

> Example:
> using the summary command
> Residual Deviance: 28034.88 on 171237 degrees of freedom

That's a very large number of df, so let me guess that this is Bernouilli
logistic regression, that is one 0/1 observation per point.  The theory
that says E(deviance) = df is for binomial(n_i, p_i) observations for
n_i large.  It does not work well if (n_i * p_i) are generally small.
I once had this problem and spent some time investigating it. As
(np) falls for 5, the expected value rises (so for np near one there
is apparent over-dispersion) and then falls rapidly (so for np ~ 0.1
there is apparent under-dispersion).

As I said, this is a guess and the conclusion above applied to my problem
(a small-area health study with ca 10,000 units), but do not treat it as
appropriate to yours.  A quick check would be to simulate some data and see
if you see the bias there too.

> I don't know how to deal with this problem in Splus.
> 
> In order to understand the logistic regression technique, I have been 
> reading a book by D. Collett titled "Modeling Binary Data".  This book 
> mentions a method for modeling overdispersion in binomial data which Collett 
> calls the Williams procedure (page 196).  I don't know if it is correct to 
> use the Williams procedure to correct for underdispersed data, and if it is, 
> how to implement the procedure in Splus.

Sorry, I don't think it is appropriate.  Under-dispersion needs negative
correlation in the observations, and that is hard to explain (even if you
are Fisher investigating Mendel, as a classic case of under-dispersed
binomial data).

messages.subject: Re: [S] Partial case translation in a string.
messages.subject_clean: [S] Partial case translation in a string.
messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ users,

Here is a summary of the answers to my question concerning partial case
translation in a string.

Many thanks to James Holtman, Colin Goodall, Greg Snow, Marcus Lee, Sam
Buttrey and Chuck Taylor.

QUESTION:

        I am doing string substitutions using PERL (www.perl.org) following
a suggestion by Prof. Brian Ripley on this list.
        I would like to know how to change the case of only a part of the
string analysed.

        Example:

             "Sample s at 120K - operator o"           (relatively free
format)
        is replaced by
             "s.120.o"
        using the PERL script
             "s/Sample (.+) at (.+)K - operator (.+)/$1\.$2\.$3/"

        I would like "S.120.o" as the final result for compatibility with
preceding observations.
        Note that using in addition the "tr/a-z/A-Z/" command leads to
"S.120.O" with a wrong ending case.
        ...
        Thank you for any help (including a not too complicated S+-only
solution).

ANSWERS:

1) Using "\U" and "\E" in PERL (by James Holtman, Colin Goodall):

        "s/Sample (.+) at (.+)K - operator (.+)/\U$1\E\.$2\.$3/"

2) Another PERL solution + how to interface with PERL (by Greg Snow):

        try the Perl command:
        s/Sample (.+) at (.+)K - operator (.+)/join('.',uc($1),$2,$3)/e

        the final e says to take the substitution part (right side) and
evaluate
        it and use the result as the substitution.  The uc function does the
upper
        case for you (and even the potential to work on characters with
accents
        etc.) and this way it is only applied to the first substring, not
all of
        them (also look at ucfirst).

        S+ does have a regexp function that can be used with the substr
function
        to do this, but it has nowhere near the same power as Perl does.
Unless
        you really need an S+ only soulution, are paying penance for losing
a bet,
        or really want to develope obscure and little needed programming
skills, I
        would stick with doing this in Perl.  One thing that could help is
Patrick
        Burns in his "S Poetry" provides an interface between S+ and Perl
(you
        call the function in S+, it does all the work behind the scenes so
you can
        pretend that you never leave S+, but still have the power of Perl).
You
        can download "S Poetry" for free from: 
        http://www.seanet.com/~pburns/Spoetry

3) Still another PERL solution (by Marcus Lee):

        #---- Start of program -------------------------------------
        #!/usr/bin/perl -w

        my ($sample,$size,$operator);

        while(<>) {

          chomp;  # remove End_of_Line character

          if ( /^\s*Sample (.+) at ([0-9]+)K - operator (.+)\s*/ ) {
            $sample   = $1;
            $size     = $2;
            $operator = $3;
            $sample   =~ tr/a-z/A-Z/;
            print "$sample.$size.$operator\n";
          }
          else {
            die "unexpected input encountered: $_\n";
          }
        }
        #---- End of program ---------------------------------------

4) Using unpaste (Sam Buttrey):

        unlist (unpaste ("Sample s at 120K - operator o", sep=" "))

        returns the words of the string (of course, "-" counts as a word
here). If
        you know that you want words 1, 2,  and 7, you can paste those back
        together:

        paste (unlist (unpaste ("Sample s at 120K - operator o", sep="
"))[c(2, 4,
        7)], collapse=".")

        gives

        [1] "s.120K.o"

        If you really can't stand the "K" in the middle, you could strip
that off in
        an intermediate step:

        thing <- unlist (unpaste ("Sample s at 120K - operator o", sep="
        "))[c(2,4,7)]
        thing[2] <- substring (thing[2], 1, nchar(thing[2]) - 1)
        paste (thing, collapse=".")

5) Converting string into a vector (Chuck Taylor):

        My usual approach to string manipulation in S is to convert the
        string to a vector, use vector operations, then convert back. 
        Here are three little functions which can be used to solve this
        problem: 

        "str.to.vec" <- function(string)
        {
                unlist(string.to.chars(string))
        }

        "vec.to.str" <- function(vec)
        {
                paste(vec, collapse = "")
        }

        "CapLeading" <- function(string) {
            temp <- str.to.vec(string)
            temp[1] <- casefold(temp[1], upper=T)
            vec.to.str(temp)
        }

messages.subject: Re: [S] Assignment operator in S-Plus
messages.body_plain:
I am one of those who is a firm devotee of the `` <- '' notation, and
I can say with a completely clear conscience that I have NEVER (in
almost 20 years of using S/SPlus) had an error due to writing
``x<-1'' when I meant ``x < -1'' or vice versa.  The reason is
visibly obvious from the foregoing --- I put ***spaces*** into my
code where appropriate.  I write ``x <- 1'' when that's what I mean.
In general, not just when avoiding ambiguity with the <- construct,
spaces are a Good Idea.  They make code much easier to read and much
more aesthetically pleasing.

Those who insist on using the (ugly) underscore notation should at
the very least write ``x _ 42'' rather than ``x_42'' (which looks to
me like it should mean entry 42 in a sequence of x-s).

The constructed arrow notation is pleasantly evocative of the
``flow'' of data from one object to another.  It would of course be
better if there were a unipartite arrow on the keyboard so that one
did not have to construct an arrow.  On some old terminal/keyboard
combinations (I think the steam-age Tektronix ``graphics''
oscilloscope style terminals were among these) the underscore
actually did print as an arrow  --- presumably this is the reason
that the underscore symbol is used as an alternative notation for the
assignment operator.

However this is not an ideal world and there is no such key nowadays,
so we make do as best we can, and IMHO the <- construction is the
best.

                                        cheers,

                                                Rolf Turner
                                                rolf at math.unb.ca

>>>>> "AZ" == Alan Zaslavsky <zaslavsk at hcp.med.harvard.edu> writes:
   At the almost certain risk of being jumped on by many (or worse yet,
   starting a long and unproductive debate), I ask why a syntax is
   considered desirable in which
      x> -1
   is a logical expression for a comparison and
        x<-1
   reassigns the value of x ?

Anyone who type "x>-1" and "x<-1" instead of "x > -1" and "x <- 1" deserves
whatever misfortune befalls him.

Underscores (in C) and dots (in S) in variable names are also an abomination.
These are both case-sensitive languages, so you should take advantage of that
to write

aVeryLongVariableName

rather than

a_very_long_variable_name  (in C)

or

a.very.long.variable.name (in S).

Jeff

bootstrapping after model fitting. There were many great replies from Vito,

using:
a<-bootstrap(data.frame,coef(glm(fit)),B=1000,trace=F)
followed by,

Warning messages:
  z0 is outside range (-.25, .25), this indicates extreme bias, assumptions 
underlying BCa interval may be violated in: limits.bca(object, probs,

Does anyone know why this would occur? Or, how I can rectify the problem? I 
know that others have received this same message and apologize if the

messages.subject: [S] Bootstrap Question
messages.body_plain:
I am fitting a generalized model to daily data that extends over a number
of years.  I want to be able to bootstrap the regression coefficients (and
perhaps other stats) within groups (years) but also by blocks of say consecutive
three day periods to preserve serial correlation known to exit.   The data looks
something like this:

   Date       Yr        Ozone         Temp           Wspd      Other variables
   June 1     94           100             72                3.4
........
   June 2     94             85             88                4.3
........
   June 3     94             .                   .                    .
.....
     ........
   Oct 30     99            120            76                4.5
.........

 One form of the model being evaluated is:

  Ozfit <- glm(Ozone ~ ns(temp,5) + ns(wspd,5 ) + .... + ns(yr,5),
family=quasi(link=log),  data= ..  )
I can bootstrap the reg coefficients nicely with

  Ozfit.boot <-     bootstrap(data = ..., statistic = coef(eval(Ozfit$call)), B
= 200, group = yr)

Is there some way I can use the bootstrap function (or the boot function from
statlib), to handle the serial correlation, e.g. bootsrap blocks of days so that
each block of days would be sampled rather than each day?    Any other
suggestions for handling this issue are welcome.  I am using Splus Pro 2000
release 2.  Thanks.

messages.body_plain:
Below is a summary to my question about Netscape and the 
help.start() facility in 5.1.  My original posting is included at the end
of the message.

It turns out the helpfile windows can be closed using keystroke
alternatives.  A couple of my collegues informed me of this.  One of
my problems was that I was using Splus via an X-windows interface on
a Mac.  It turns out the default keyboard settings have the Alt key
turned off so the keystrokes weren't working.

However, using Alt-w to close a Netscape window and Alt-p to print
worked just fine on our PCs and workstations.

Thanks to Gardar Johannesson, Mark Irwin and Michaels Ernst for
their help.

Also, Peter Perkins suggested the following:

> Is there some options that can be set to get
> the File Edit View etc.. menubar to show up in the individual
> helpfile windows?

try this: in $SHOME/splus/lib/X11/helpstart, replace the line

   open(url,"srch_trm","width=800,height=500,resizable=1,
      scrolling=1,menubar=1,scrollbars=1");

with the line

   open(url,"srch_trm","width=600,height=500,resizable=1,
      scrolling=1,statusbar=1,location=1,scrollbars=1");

(without line breaks).  this is documented at

   http://home.netscape.com/newsref/std/x-remote.html

Thanks for all the suggestions.

Nicole

messages.subject: [S] CFP: Internet Imaging
messages.body_plain:
(Our apologies if multiple copies arrive you.)

                        Internet Imaging (EI14)
                                part of
            Electronic Imaging 2001, Science and Technology

                         21 to 26 January 2001
                       San Jose, California, USA

Internet Imaging II (EI24)

Conference Chairs: Giordano Beretta, Hewlett-Packard Co.; Raimondo
Schettini, Istituto Tecnologie Informatiche Multimediali, CNR (Italy)
Program Committee: Robert R. Buckley, Xerox Corp.; Shih-Fu Chang, Columbia
Univ.; Lucy Cherkasova, Hewlett-Packard Labs.; Alberto Del Bimbo, Univ.
degli Studi di Firenze (Italy); Ullas Gargi, Hewlett-Packard Labs.; Theo
Gevers, Univ. of Amsterdam (Netherlands); Jennifer Gille, Raytheon ITSS;
Neil J. Gunther, Performance Dynamics Consulting; Roger-David Hersch, École
Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (Switzerland); Yasuyo G. Ichihara, Hosen
Gakuen Junior College (Japan); Corinne Jörgensen, SUNY/Buffalo; Lloyd
McIntyre, Xerox Corp.; Marco Padula, Istituto Tecnologie Informatiche
Multimediali, CNR (Italy); Simon Shim, San Jose State Univ.; Maureen Stone,
StoneSoup Consulting; Sabine E. Süsstrunk, École Polytechnique Fédérale de
Lausanne (Switzerland); Ingeborg Tastl, Sony Electronics Inc.; Alain
Trémeau, Univ. Jean Monnet (France); Robert A. Ulichney, Compaq Computer
Corp.; Yujin Zhang, Tsinghua Univ. (China)

Images have been the main propellant for the Internet's popularization.
Expectations for performance and quality of images are driving new
technologies as the space of web-connected business and commercial
imaging solutions grows and as the cost of Web access and high quality
reproduction hardcopy devices drops. New applications are appearing to
take advantage of these opportunities, and exposing new system
requirements.

Internet imaging is different from other imaging applications because an
internet is a network of networks. This entails complications like
unpredictable latency, caching, firewalls, security, platform
heterogeneity, standardization, and others. Furthermore, images can be
still images, animations, or video sequences.

This conference is intended as a forum for discussing these
technologies, applications, and challenges facing them. The participants
will present the most recent developments in the appropriate
representation, communication, and rendering of images using the
Internet. Focus of the conference is on novel means of image capture,
coding, computation and representation specific to the Internet,
efficient transport of images over networks, display and rendering of
image received over networks, and the requirements of applications which
derive value from the use of these technologies. Unmet needs of desired
applications are also relevant. Algorithms, protocols, software,
hardware, communications systems, and applications are appropriate
topics.

Papers are solicited in the following areas, and special attention is
given to new applications and requirements created by opportunities on
the Internet:

*) image processing for Internet, reuse of softcopy and hardcopy images:
data compression and representation, coding for multiresolution or
resolution-independent images
*) imaging issues in content-based indexing, search and retrieval,
indexing video
*) virtual and augmented reality, telemedicine, data visualization,
remote surveillance
*) Internet video, multimedia presentation on the Internet: multimedia
integration, presentation, management, authoring, animation, SMIL, SVG,
VRML, Interactive TV, multimedia presentation formats, presentation
agents, and e-commerce

messages.subject: RE: [S] Underdispered data in logistic regression - request for SPlus code.
messages.subject_clean: [S] Underdispered data in logistic regression - request for SPlus code.
messages.body_plain:
I think this may be of wider interest. If you have not seen it you may be
surprised by the bias for moderate n or lambda.  The Chi-squared measure of
fit is a lot more reliable as a test for under/over-dispersion.

On Fri, 12 May 2000, Sorkin, John wrote:

> Prof Ripley,
> 
> Would you have SPlus code that can be used to explore the relation between
> the E(dispersion) and n and p? If you do, would you mind sharing the code
> with me? I believe I could learn a lot by reviewing the relation.

I did this before S-PLUS existed (c 1985).  However, for a Poisson
response try

x <- 0:100
pp <- function(lambda)
  sum(dpois(x, lambda) *2 * ( (lambda - x) + x * log(pmax(1,x)/lambda)))
lambda <- c(0.01, 0.05, seq(0.1, 5, 0.1))
plot(lambda, sapply(lambda, pp), type="l", ylim=c(0, 1.2), ylab = "E(deviance)")
abline(h=1, lty=3)

and for a binomial

n <- 1
pp <- function(p, n)
{
  y <- (0:n)/n
  devy <- sum(dbinom(1:n, n, p) * y[-1] * log(y[-1])) +
          sum(dbinom(1:n, n, 1-p) * y[-1] * log(y[-1]))
  devmu <- sum(dbinom(0:n, n, p) * (y * log(p) + (1-y)*log(1-p)))
  2 *n * (devy - devmu)
}
p <- seq(0.01, 0.99, 0.01)
plot(p, sapply(p, pp, n=n), type="l", ylab = "E(deviance)")
for(n in 2:10) lines(p, sapply(p, pp, n=n), type="l")
lines(p, sapply(p, pp, n=25), type="l")
abline(h=1, lty=3)

--

messages.body_plain:
A related reference to Brian's neat little demo, coming to the same
conclusion but with more detail on the alternatives, is the following,
(the reference by courtesy of CIS):

@String{JASA={Journal of the American Statistical Association}}

@Article{Larn:78:SCE,
 Author = {Larntz, Kinley},
 Title  = {{Small-sample} Comparisons of Exact Levels for 
{Chi-squared}
    Goodness-of-fit Statistics},
 Journal= JASA,
 Year   = 1978,
 Volume = 73,
 Pages  = {253--263},
 Keyword= {Pearson chi-squared test, Likelihood ratio test, 
Freeman-Tukey
    statistic, Categorical data},
}

--

I have always thought that a test-of-fit statistic with binary data
was always going to be a pretty folorn hope since the deviance is
really a likelihood ratio test of the present model within a saturated
alternative, that is, one that grows in degrees of freedom as the
sample size increases and hence standard LR theory is out the window.

It has always seemed more realistic to me to pick a fairly large but
fixed alternative rather than a saturated one, but still likely to
pick up most serious forms of fit deficiency.  Of course this is
exactly what you are doing if you have repeated covariate sets in your
binary data and you group them into binomial data and agree to limit
the covariate sets under consideration to those you currently have,
but the idea is more general.  Of course this raises the question of
how well *differences* of deviances behave relative to their notional
chi-squared null distribution and most of the work I have seen on this
seems to suggest that for most practical purposes they perform pretty
well.  I'm not aware of any comprehensive studies, though.

If this were not the case we might have to revive all that old work on
"exact" partitioning of Pearson's Chi-squared statistic that was such
a fashion at one stage.  There are even some faint signs it may be in
a minor revival already.  Here's a recent article, again from CIS:

@String{AusNZJSt={The Australian and New Zealand Journal of 
Statistics}}

@Article{Beh:Davy:98:PPC,
 Author = {Beh, Eric J. and Davy, Pamela J.},
 Title  = {{Partitioning} {Pearson's} Chi-squared Statistic for a 
Completely
    Ordered Three-way Contingency Table},
 Journal= AusNZJSt,
 Year   = 1998,
 Volume = 40,
 Pages  = {465--477},
 Keyword= {Log-linear model},
}

--

It turns out that the order of the open statements should be reversed in
my previous posting.  You want to replace

   open(url,"srch_trm","width=600,height=500,resizable=1,
      scrolling=1,statusbar=1,location=1,scrollbars=1");

with

   open(url,"srch_trm","width=800,height=500,resizable=1,
      scrolling=1,menubar=1,scrollbars=1");

to get a full menu in the help topic window when using help.start().

Peter Perkins clarifies a few things below:

[snip]
> 
> this is documented at
> 
> http://home.netscape.com/newsref/std/x-remote.html
> 
i just realized that the mod i suggested in all.html is actually pure
javascript.  the url i referred to above documents the call help.start()
makes to bring up the initial help page in netscape.

i also just realized that i had the old and new lines mixed up -- the one
with "menubar=1" is what you need to get a full menubar in the help topic
window, which buys you printing for one.  sufficient knowledge of
javascript
should also allow one to get a new window each time.  grabbing the
filename
from the url arg should suffice.

man, i _really_ was not paying enough attention.

- peter

[snip]

try this: in $SHOME/splus/lib/X11/helpstart, replace the line

messages.subject: [S] split() a dataframe for summary stats
messages.subject_clean: [S] split() a dataframe for summary stats
messages.body_plain:
I recently purchased a copy of Krause and Olson's The Basics of S and 
S-Plus (2nd ed.), and was startled to see on page 181 an example of 
split() applied to a dataframe. For example (not their example):

> foo <- data.frame(a=I( c('a','a','a','b','b')) ,
                    x=1:5,
                    date=as(1231:1235,'timeDate') )
> foo
  a x    date
1 a 1 5-15-63
2 a 2 5-16-63
3 a 3 5-17-63
4 b 4 5-18-63
5 b 5 5-19-63

> fspl <- split(foo,foo$a)
> fspl
$a:
    a   x      date
1 "a" "1" "5-15-63"
2 "a" "2" "5-16-63"
3 "a" "3" "5-17-63"

$b:
    a   x      date
4 "b" "4" "5-18-63"
5 "b" "5" "5-19-63"

> fspl$a
  a x    date
1 a 1 5-15-63
2 a 2 5-16-63
3 a 3 5-17-63

As far as I know, this is an undocumented feature. The help page on 
split() specifies a vector for the first argument to split. I hope it 
continues to be a feature in future versions.

This feature immediately suggests a potential solution to what has 
long been a vexing (to me) omission from Splus. That is, the ability 
to perform aggregations that summarize more than one variable. For 
example, one might want to find the maximum of x within each subset 
as defined by a, and at the same time find the date on which the 
maximum occurred.

Continuing with the example:

Note that each element of the list returned by split() has the same 
structure as the original.

We gave split() a data frame, each element of the list it returns is 
a dataframe:

> sapply(fspl,class)
            a            b
 "data.frame" "data.frame"
>

The columns of each data frame are of the same class as the original:
> sapply(fspl$a,class)
      a         x       date
 "AsIs" "integer" "timeDate"
> sapply(foo,class)
      a         x       date
 "AsIs" "integer" "timeDate"
>
(note that if a had been of class 'character' it would now be a 
factor; using I() gave it class 'asis', which is preserved)

To summarize each subset as described above:

> tmpfun <- function(df)
> data.frame(a=df$a[1],max=max(df$x),date=df$date[df$x==max(df$x)])

> fsum <- lapply(fspl,tmpfun)
> fsum
$a:
    a max      date
1 "a" "3" "5-17-63"

$b:
    a max      date
1 "b" "5" "5-19-63"

Despite appearances, the elements aren't all character strings:

> fsum$a
  a max    date
1 a   3 5-17-63

> sapply(fsum,class)
            a            b
 "data.frame" "data.frame"

> sapply(fsum$a,class)
      a       max       date
 "AsIs" "integer" "timeDate"
>

The result of lapply() is a list. Each element of the list is a 
dataframe, whose elements have classes that are the same as the 
variable they summarize. Finally, we make a dataframe out of the list:

> fsum.df <- do.call('rbind',fsum)
> fsum.df
  a max    date
a a   3 5-17-63
b b   5 5-19-63
> class(fsum.df)
[1] "data.frame"
> sapply(fsum.df,class)
      a       max       date
 "AsIs" "integer" "timeDate"
>

Some caveats:

First-

I don't know for certain this feature of split() is undocumented. But 
here is what the help page in Splus 5.1 says:

"data: vector containing data values to be grouped. Missing values ( 
NAs) are allowed."

Second-

Having said all this, I think I need to take another look at Hmisc's 
summary.formula(). It may be able to do this kind of aggregation, and 
I just never realized it. If so, it looks like summary.formula() is 
much more general and powerful than this approach. I don't know of 
any Splus-supplied functions to do this kind of aggregation (have I 
somehow missed one?)

Finally, this approach might be painfully slow with large datasets.

-Don
--------------------------------
Don MacQueen
Environmental Protection Dept.
Livermore, CA, USA
Lawrence Livermore National Lab
--------------------------------

messages.subject: [S] importing from Excel: WARNING!
messages.body_plain:
running S-PLUS 2000 on Windows 98

At first I was quite pleased to see that S-PLUS 2000
would import Excel files.  My primary databases all
export to Excel, anad the conversion therefrom to
.csv for reading into S-PLUS was exceedingly tiresome.

Last week someone pointed out to me an error 
in some results I prepared using S-PLUS.  Investigating,
I discovered that "import.data" was converting my character
data to factors without warning.  I was aware of "as.is=T"
option for "read.table", and took pains to look for this
when reading the helpfile for "import.data".  To no avail.
This undocumented feature (=BUG!) of "import.data"
can be remedied by the equally undocumented option
StringsAsFactors="Never" but, alas, I had already my
submitted my report.  So I had to issue a mea culpa,
retract the report, and start over. 

Now I find that I must issue another mea culpa, retract
the revision, and start over yet again.   Boy, does 
S-PLUS really increase my productivity and make
me look good!  :(

It seems that when S-PLUS reads an Excel file, it will
only read the first 32 characters of any field.  Some of
my fields have more than 32 characters, differ only
in the characters 33 and beyond and, consequently,
all my matches, etc. are incorrect.  My results are
worthless.

Apparently, so it was explained to me by tech support,
the 32 character limitation is imposed by the GUI.  Yet,
when I read from ASCII files, I get all my characters,
not just the first 32.

If S-PLUS claims to import Excel files, it should import
the entire file, not just part of it.

I'd love to continue, but I have to spend yet another week
redoing something I've already done twice, and convince
the powers-that-be that S-PLUS really is a good package,
that this was a (twice) atypical occurrence, yada yada yada...

Regards,

Bruce

messages.subject: [S] Bootstrapping samples of unequal size
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-users,

I would like to compare the means of two samples, the second sample taken 
from the first. The first sample has n=1380 observations and the subset 
(from the first sample) has n=133. Essentially I would like to bootstrap 
the difference of the two sample means to see if the mean from the second 
sample is "different" than it's parent (to see if zero lies outside of the 
95% CI interval). Has anyone created code for this before? I am relatively 
new to using S-plus and haven't had much success. Any help would be 
appreciated and I will post any replies to the list.
Thanks in advance,
Daniel

messages.subject: [S] Looking for help with time series analyses
messages.subject_clean: [S] Looking for help with time series analyses
messages.body_plain:
To those out there familiar with time series analysis:

I am a graduate student in Physical Geography at UC Berkeley and have
successfully collected a very large volume of time series data on
intertidal wetlands hydrology that I am beginning to analyze closely for
my dissertation. I am looking for folks with whom I can correspond to
help me understand analyzing these data within the SPlus environment. I
just completed the 4-day SPlus training course, which got me going on
the software but never touched upon doing the time series analyses. In
addition to purchasing SPlus 2000, I also bought the wavelets module
version 1.1.

Here's a synopsis of the data:
1. Parameters include water level (3 locations), suspended sediment
concentration (2 locations), average velocity (2 locations, 3
dimensions), turbulent velocity (2 locations, 3 dimensions), and bottom
elevation (2 locations).
2. Sampling intervals are generally 12 minutes.
3. Duration of data collection is about 2 years.
4. Water level, suspended sediment, and bottom elevation yield
single-point measurements per sampling interval; velocity yields 24
measurements for the average (sampled at 0.2 Hz) and between 1,200 and
3,000 measurements for the turbulent (sampled at 25 Hz for varying
durations depending on how I programmed the instruments).

These data are inherently serially correlated, so my analyses must
address this condition. I have a number of hypotheses I plan to test.

I am working on a Windows 98 PC with a fair bit of processing power (K7
550 MHz, 256mb RAM).

Many thanks in advance for those that have the expertise to offer me a
little help.

Stuart Siegel
UC Berkeley Department of Geography
siegel at socrates.berkeley.edu OR stuart at swampthing.org

messages.subject_clean: [S] Permanent Research Fellow position, Applied mathematics & Computer science. Cemagref LISC
messages.body_plain:
<Sorry for multiple delivery - please disseminate to potential
candidates>

The LISC team (Laboratory for complex systems engineering) of Cemagref
(french public research institute for agriculture and environment) in
Clermont-Ferrand proposes a Permanent Research Fellow
position (civil servant, CR2) in Applied mathematics & Computer science.

The recruitment conditions and the corresponding submission
forms can be downloaded (as pdf files) at :
        
http://www.cemagref.fr/Informations/Actualites/Concours/charges-recherche.htm

European as well as non-European candidates welcome.

Please note that applicants will be asked to come in Paris, France for
an oral presentation.
xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
!!!! VERY IMPORTANT-- VERY SHORT DEADLINES -- submission forms must be
sent before May, 22 !!!
xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx

Description of the position 

Level: Chargé de Recherches. This is a Permanent post-doctoral Research
Fellow position and a French civil servant position.
Research Domain : Applied mathematics & Computer science
Location : Clermont-Ferrand (centre of France)

Details of the Position

The successful applicant will work in the LISC team (Laboratory for
complex systems engineering) of Cemagref (French public research
institute for agriculture and environment). This team is involved in
building
simulation models simulate of the dynamics of complex systems, such as
hydrosystems, aquatic
ecosystems, social interactions in rural areas, agricultural systems and
food processing. The main objective is eventually to achieve the
integration of
these models in management support tools (decision and negotiation) for
these 
complex systems. 

We are particularly interested in defining generic classes of models
that can be used in various application domains. These models are
characterised by a local definition of the dynamics, which is often
spatially explicit. At a global level, dynamic shapes can be defined and
studied at various scales. The main research theme in LISC deals with
the characterisation and modelling of the dynamics of such shapes, at
the relevant scale. We also study which actions should be applied on
these dynamics in order to satisfy ecological, economic or social
objectives. For example, we study the impact of (or we define) policies,
practices or techniques which could make the structure of a rural area
evolve, taking into account the combined objectives within agricultural
production, landscape management, water quality improvement and aquatic
ecosystems conservation.

The collaboration of various disciplines is often necessary to fulfil
these objectives. Researchers building such models therefore need a
capacity to work in an interdisciplinary context.

Description of the research activities:

The successful applicant will develop mathematical methods to study and 
simulate the dynamics of such systems in collaboration with the
other members of the team.

Such research would be carried out in strong collaboration with
specialists of the appropriate domains (ecology, hydrology, sociology,
rural development and food processing), and will lead to the development
of applied software.

A significant part of this research will take place within European
Projects.

The researcher will potentially be responsible for a team of
undergraduate and graduate students, in methodological and applied
aspects. He/she is also be expected to take part in the scientific
debates within the team and the institute, as appropriate to his/her
research domain.

Required Qualifications and Skills

*  PhD in applied mathematics or computer science, preferably
centred on theoretical and methodological aspects of the dynamics of
spatial systems.
*  Capacity to supervise Masters students, to take part in the
training of PhD students and to initiate projects.
*  Ability to communicate and to work well within a team.
*  Good level of English.
*  Some knowledge of, or ability in,  distributed models (multi
agent systems, automata networks, lattice gaz), and/or of geographical
information systems (GIS) would also be appreciated.
*  To be less than 32 year old

Salary complies with the grid of French public sector ($1500 - $2000 a
month).  

Please feel free to contact Guillaume Deffuant, the lab. Leader for any
additional information
e-mail : guillaume.deffuant at cemagref.fr

messages.subject: Re: [S] Bootstrapping samples of unequal size
messages.body_plain:
Dear Daniel Rainham,

I find your problem a little confusing.  Are you selecting 133 cases
out of 1380 on the basis of some characteristic that distinguishes
them, so that you are estimating the difference in means between
two groups, based on sample sizes of 133 and 1247?  If so, this
is a familiar and clear two-sample problem.  The difference in
sample size does not cause any great difficulty.  It is not clear,
however, what motivates the use of bootstrap methods for this
particular problem.

The way you worded the problem, however, it sounds more like a class
exercise, in which the 1380 observations define a population with
known mean and the 133 cases are randomly sampled from it.  One could
take many such random samples, in order to estimate the sampling
distribution of the mean empirically; and for some of the samples,
one could also get a bootstrap estimate of the sampling distribution
of the mean, in order to compare bootstrap estimates of a sampling
distribution with the (directly approximated) true distribution.
If that is what you are doing, it is a rather different problem.

Either way, Splus code for bootstrapping is not so hard to write,
at least for experienced programmers.  Some clarification of the logic
of the problem and the reason for taking the bootstrap approach (scientific
reasons versus class exercise) might be in order, before anyone offers
actual help.

Dave Krantz

> I would like to compare the means of two samples, the second sample taken 
> from the first. The first sample has n=1380 observations and the subset 
> (from the first sample) has n=133. Essentially I would like to bootstrap 
> the difference of the two sample means to see if the mean from the second 
> sample is "different" than it's parent (to see if zero lies outside of the 
> 95% CI interval). Has anyone created code for this before? I am relatively 
> new to using S-plus and haven't had much success. Any help would be 
> appreciated and I will post any replies to the list.
> Thanks in advance,
> Daniel

> Daniel.G.C. Rainham
> Climate and Health Research Program
> Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences
> University of Alberta
