messages.subject: [S] mixed-mode multivariate summary statistics
messages.body_plain:
I've often wished for a function that would do mixed-mode 
multivariate summary statistics, and return the results as a 
dataframe. By this I mean, for example, for each subset of the data, 
as defined by a set of several grouping variables, find the range of 
x, the proportion of k=='big', the maximum of y, and the subject 
associated with the maximum of y.

Thanks to input from several sources, including Krause & Olson's book 
"The Basics of S and S-Plus", Venables & Ripley's MASS and new book 
"S Programming", and Frank Harrell's Hmisc, I've finally found an 
easy way to do this, which I think is worth sharing.

----- Here is some example data, and an appropriate function ----

mydat <- data.frame(
           grp1=c(rep('a',5),rep('b',3), 'c','c' ),
           grp2=rep( c('m','f'),c(5,5) ),
           subject=I(LETTERS[1:10]),
           k=rep(c('big','small'),c(7,3)),
           date=as(1301:1310,'timeDate'),
           x=21:30,
           y=1:10
           )
myfun <- function(df) {
  data.frame(
    grp1=df$grp1[1],
    grp2=df$grp2[1],
    n=nrow(df),
    pk=signif(sum(df$k=='big')/nrow(df),3),
    xlo=min(df$x),
    xhi=max(df$x),
    ymax=max(df$y),
    subject=df$subject[df$y==max(df$y)],
    mindate=min(df$date),
    maxdate=max(df$date)
    )
}

---- And here is how to do the summary ----

myby <- by(mydat,list(grp1=mydat$grp1,grp2=mydat$grp2),myfun)
mysum <- do.call('rbind',myby)

---- And the results ----

> mydat
   grp1 grp2 subject     k    date  x  y
 1    a    m       A   big 7-24-63 21  1
 2    a    m       B   big 7-25-63 22  2
 3    a    m       C   big 7-26-63 23  3
 4    a    m       D   big 7-27-63 24  4
 5    a    m       E   big 7-28-63 25  5
 6    b    f       F   big 7-29-63 26  6
 7    b    f       G   big 7-30-63 27  7
 8    b    f       H small 7-31-63 28  8
 9    c    f       I small  8-1-63 29  9
10    c    f       J small  8-2-63 30 10
> mysum
  grp1 grp2 n    pk xlo xhi ymax subject mindate maxdate
1    b    f 3 0.667  26  28    8       H 7-29-63 7-31-63
2    c    f 2 0.000  29  30   10       J  8-1-63  8-2-63
3    a    m 5 1.000  21  25    5       E 7-24-63 7-28-63
>
-------------------------------------------------------
This approach has some advantages:
  It is _very_ simple
  The mode of the original data is easily preserved
  [check this with sapply(mydat,class) and sapply(msum,class)]

It has disadvantages (I suspect)
  It appears to be slow
  Memory usage may be a problem with large datasets

For summaries of numeric variables only, I would recommend 
summarize() or summary.formula() in Hmisc, or Splus's aggregate() for 
time series. Or the traditional lapply(), tapply() if you don't need 
results returned in a dataframe with the grouping variables included 
as columns.

One has to be careful how the function passed to by() is defined. The 
group variables have to be returned, of course. If it returns a 
dataframe with more than one row, watch out!

If someone has a better way, I'd sure appreciate hearing about it.

-------------------------------------------------------

Some comments

Note that the order of the grouping variables in the summary is not 
what one might expect (apparently, alphabetical grp2, then grp1 
within grp2). A nice little exercise is to modify the command mysum 
<- do.call('rbind',myby) to alphabetize grp2 within grp1. It's worth 
looking at the structure of the object myby.

-------------------------------------------------------

Some ruminations (stop here if you're not feeling very philosophical)

Strictly speaking, S is a computational language, specialized for 
data analysis and graphics. However, S-Plus competes with the likes 
of SAS, SPSS, and Stata. SAS has had this kind of capability for many 
years.

In my field, environmental statistics in a regulatory context, data 
preparation is typically 70 to 80 percent of the job; actual data 
analysis or statistics is a relatively small proportion. In the past 
I've used SAS for data prep and Splus for data analysis and graphics. 
I'd like to do everything in Splus, but Splus is weak in data 
preparation. These kinds of summaries are essential for data 
preparation.

-Don
--------------------------------
Don MacQueen
Environmental Protection Dept.
Livermore, CA, USA
Lawrence Livermore National Lab
--------------------------------

messages.subject: [S] frailty model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a problem in correlated survival data. I hope you can give me some
direction on how to approach this problem using splus. Here is the problem:

I have 200 siblings who were bron around 1900 from 45 families, among them,
8 are still alive (censored). The question is if the survival curve of
these 200 persons is different from a known standard survival curve. I plan
to use us life table to construct a known standard survival curve. Since
most of the frailty models are used in the clinical trial data with two (or
more) treatment groups with covariates, I am interested in see if other
people have already done similar studies which were using a one-sample test
that adjusts for the correlation among siblings from the same families
(using marginal or random effect model). Is there any splus or SAS codes
can be used for this problem with some revision?

In splus, I can use "survdiff" with "offset" option to do a one sample
test, however, I don't know how to incorporate the random effect (W) in
such model. On the opposite, "coxph" can handle the random frailty effect
by "offset(W)" option, where W is the random frailty effect. But I don't
know how to use "coxph" to do a one sample test.

Your help will be greatly appreciated!

James

messages.subject: [S] subsetting dataframes
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a data frame that contains within it two variables, the subject
number (subjno) and the family number (famno) since some of the
subjects are siblings.  I would like to be able to access subsets of
this data frame in a couple different ways.

Assume the following example data set:

data.df = data.frame(subjno=c(2,3,5,7,8,9,10,12,13,15),
                     famno=c(2,2,4,6,6,7,7,9,11,12),
                     v1=1:10,
                     v2=11:20)

> data.df
   subjno famno v1 v2 
 1      2     2  1 11
 2      3     2  2 12
 3      5     4  3 13
 4      7     6  4 14
 5      8     6  5 15
 6      9     7  6 16
 7     10     7  7 17
 8     12     9  8 18
 9     13    11  9 19
10     15    12 10 20

i)  Suppose I want to look at the data for subjects 2,3 and 7.  Is
    there a more elegant way to access their data than the following?

    good <- match(c(2,3,7), data.df$subjno, nomatch=0)
    data.df[good, ]

      subjno famno v1 v2 
    1      2     2  1 11
    2      3     2  2 12
    4      7     6  4 14

ii) What I am particulary interested in accomplishing is the same
    thing but grab data according to family number.  The above method
    using match() will not work since famno is not unique.  match(x,y)
    will only return the indice of the *first* element in y that
    matches x. 

    For example, suppose I want to access the data for subjects with
    family numbers 2, 6 and 11.  Is there a *simpler* way than the
    following? 

    attach(data.df)
    tmp.df <- data.df[famno==2, ]
    for(i in c(6,11)) tmp.df <- rbind(tmp.df, data.df[famno==i,])
    detach("data.df")
    tmp.df

      subjno famno v1 v2 
    1      2     2  1 11
    2      3     2  2 12
    4      7     6  4 14
    5      8     6  5 15
    9     13    11  9 19

Thanks for any help,

Nicole

messages.subject: [S] mixed logistic model ?
messages.body_plain:
I have some binomial data which I'd like to analyze using logistic
regression.  The catch is that I'd like to use a mixed model approach.  Is
there such a thing as mixed model logistic regression analysis?  Is there a
way to do it in S-PLUS?  Is this appropriate?

Here's a brief description of my data.  I have information on the size of
fish (length) taken from many streams (51) in several different geographics
locations (~ 10) , and I want to relate this to the probability that the
fish undergo a specific biological transformation (a binomial response,
either the fish did or did not transform).  The transformation is strongly
related to size, but the size "cutoff" at which the transformation takes
place is different for different populations (i.e., streams).  In addition
I would like to assess which model is more appropriate ... a single model
(relating length to probability of transformation) for ALL the regions or a
separate model for each region (i.e., are regional differences
significant?).  Length and region are fixed effects, and stream is a random
effect.

I'm using S-PLUS 2000 Professional Release 2 for Windows NT.
Please respond to me, and I'll summarize to the list.
Thanks for the help.

JVA

Thanks to all who responded:  Anne York, Gardar Johannesson, Chuck
Taylor, Don McKenzie, Greg Snow, Charles Berry, Bill Dunlap, 
Peter Perkins and Brad Biggerstaff.

The most common suggestion was to switch the match arguments 
and then create a logical vector:

     data.df[match(data.df$famno, c(2,6,11),0) != 0, ]

or

     data.df[!is.na(match(data.df$famno, c(2,6,11))), ]

Apparently, is.element() will do this directly:

     data.df[is.element(data.df$famno, c(2,6,11)),]

Also, Brad Biggerstaff pointed out that Frank Harrell's Hmisc library
(statlib) has the function "%in%" which can be applied in the
following way:

     data.df[data.df$famno %in% c(2,6,11),]

messages.subject: RE: [S] importing from Excel: WARNING!
messages.body_plain:
I've been in touch with Bruce directly on this, but I also wanted to alert
all of s-news about a problem with exporting character data to ASCII which
arose while looking into this.

>>From our discussions, the problem is not with *importing* data: S-PLUS 2000
Release 2 doesn't truncate any data when importing from ASCII or to Excel.
The problem arises when *exporting* data to ASCII using export.data (or File
| Export Data from the menus): S-PLUS truncates character columns to 31
characters.  The problem does not affect factor columns, nor does it affect
exporting data (factor or character) to other file types such as Excel.  If
you are exporting long character strings using ASCII, the workaround is to
convert the columns to factor first, or to use the function write.table
instead.

Many thanks to Bruce for supplying the test case which led to identifying
this problem.

# David Smith

messages.subject: Re: [S] Bootstrapping samples of unequal size - summary
messages.subject_clean: [S] Bootstrapping samples of unequal size - summary
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Prof. Ripley, Rolf Turner, Ken Banks, David Kratnz:

My poorly written inquiry received replies with some useful information for 
those interested in repeated sampling. The lesson learned here is that 
bootstrapping is not "generally" useful or applicable for situations where 
well-known, much studied tests will suffice. Here are the replies as 
promised:

>>From Prof. Ripley:

I doubt if bootstrapping is valid... the right test is whether its mean is 
different from that of a random sample.  That's easy, and not 
bootstrapping.
mean(sample(samp1, 133))  will generate the mean of a random sample
res <- numeric(1000) for(i in 1:1000) res[i] <- mean(sample(samp1, 133))
will give you 1000 sample means, and you can compare you second-sample mean 
to that population.  (You could do a formal Monte Carlo test, but it 
doesn't seem worth the bother.)
>>From Rolf Turner:
It seems to me that you simply want to re-sample from the "large" (n80) 
sample, find the means of the re-samples, and then look to see how the mean 
of your smaller sample stacks up in comparison with the re-sample means.
I.e. you only want to "bootstrap" from the big sample.  Moreover you don't 
really want to compare the means of the two samples; you want to see where 
the mean of the small sample lies in the distribution of the means of all 
possible such small samples.
Coding this is trivial; suppose your big sample is X and your small
sample is x.  Execute
        > B <- unlist(lapply(1:1000,function(i){mean(sample(X,133))}))
        > sum(B<=mean(x))/1000

This code took about 10 or 15 seconds to run on a Sun Ultra 1, running 
Splus 3.4 under Solaris 2.7.
The last line gives you the "location" in the distribution of re-sample 
means, of the mean of your small sample x.
The number of "bootstrap" samples used is 1000 which is somewhat arbitrary; 
you can change it to anything you like.  The "1000" value should be "about 
right" for most purposes.

>>From Ken Banks:
boot.obj1 <- bootstrap(Education, mean, B00)
boot.obj1

>>From David Krantz:
... this is a familiar and clear two-sample problem.  The difference in 
sample size does not cause any great difficulty.  It is not clear, however, 
what motivates the use of bootstrap methods for this particular problem.
The way you worded the problem, however, it sounds more like a class 
exercise, in which the 1380 observations define a population with known 
mean and the 133 cases are randomly sampled from it.  One could take many 
such random samples, in order to estimate the sampling distribution of the 
mean empirically; and for some of the samples, one could also get a 
bootstrap estimate of the sampling distribution of the mean, in order to 
compare bootstrap estimates of a sampling distribution with the (directly 
approximated) true distribution.  If that is what you are doing, it is a 
rather different problem.

Thanks again to all those who replied.
Daniel R.

On Wed, 17 May 2000, Sung Jin Kang wrote:

> I am using S Plus 2000 with Window NT 4. Recently I tried to import SPSS
> data of size 10.1MB. But the message is short of memory. Is there any steps
> to increase memory capability? The memory size of my computer is 128MB.

What precisely was the message?   There is a limit on the object size of
S objects, by default 5Mb I believe, so the problem might only be that you
are exceeding that (set it via options(object.size = 2e7), say).
Also, it is not clear to me how to map the size of an SPSS dataset to
a S object (it depends on what is in the data) but the size can differ
quite a lot (up or down).

Otherwise the relevant amount of memory is not the amount of RAM (which I
assume you are quoting), but the amount of virtual memory available,
including swap space but excluding that already in use by NT and other
processes.  Have Task Manager running to see what is being used.  You may
be able to increase the swap space available if needed.

messages.subject: Re: [S] mixed logistic model ?
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 16 May 2000 jean_adams at usgs.gov wrote:

> I have some binomial data which I'd like to analyze using logistic
> regression.  The catch is that I'd like to use a mixed model approach.  Is
> there such a thing as mixed model logistic regression analysis?  Is there a
> way to do it in S-PLUS?  Is this appropriate?

There certainly is such a thing, and more generally GLMMs. It is not
currently easy to do in S-PLUS, and to some extent not at all due to the
integrations that are needed.

> Here's a brief description of my data.  I have information on the size of
> fish (length) taken from many streams (51) in several different geographics
> locations (~ 10) , and I want to relate this to the probability that the
> fish undergo a specific biological transformation (a binomial response,
> either the fish did or did not transform).  The transformation is strongly

I assume that this is actually a binary response, 0/1 rather than a count,
and you want to relate the probablity of the binary response to the length
rather than v.v.?

> related to size, but the size "cutoff" at which the transformation takes
> place is different for different populations (i.e., streams).  In addition
> I would like to assess which model is more appropriate ... a single model
> (relating length to probability of transformation) for ALL the regions or a
> separate model for each region (i.e., are regional differences
> significant?).  Length and region are fixed effects, and stream is a random
> effect.

Um. Why is stream a random effect?   You are interested in the effect of
length and region, and it is usual (e.g. in anova with block designs) to
condition on incidental random effects.  Since you seem only to expecting
this to be a shift on linear predictor scale, comparing glm models

stream + length
stream + length + region
stream + length * region

ought to give valid inferences on the different fixed effects terms.
You will get some non-estimable terms if streams are nested in regions,
so a cleaner view might be

stream + length
region + stream %in% region + length
region + stream %in% region + length + region:length

and for the latter you can also fit region-specific models and sum
log-likelihoods and deviances.

There is another problem too. If streams occur within regions, and regions
are a fixed effect, streams cannot be a random effect, or at least you
will need to stratify on region.  If you want to consider random effects
you need to identify the populations from which they are drawn.

Now, if you really need random effects, I would group the data on length
groups to get binomial responses.  Then you could use lme on a linearized
version of the problem.  That is fit a binomial glm, and take out the
weights and responses from the final step of the IWLS, and use that
linearized model in lme.  (I understand that a package GLME is in the
pipeline doing this for you.)  There is an OME example in V&R3 and its
exercises doing essentially this using nlme (it is not just logistic).  
The reason for grouping is that without it the linearization may well not
be adequate.  If linearized methods are not adequate, you could use MCMC
approaches, of which for this problem there are several variants.

Another approach you could consider is GEE, that will allow correlated
responses within streams. If the simple shift-in-linear-predictor model
is adequate, this seems far too complicated to specify in correlation
terms.

[I should stress that I am much less than 100% sure that my interpretations
here of what you have are correct, and one reason for posting this answer
is that others may view the problem differently.]

--

messages.subject: Re: [S] mixed logistic model ?
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 16 May 2000, Shige Song wrote:

> Do you mean this can not currently be done in S-plus? I am new to
> S-plus, but it appears to me that there is a function called "nlme" for
> non-linear mixed models, isn't it designed to do this kind of job? Thank
> you very much.

No, it is not designed for this kind of job.  It is designed for Gaussian
non-linear mixed models.  My book with Bill Venables may help make clear to
you what nlme does.  (It is the same distinction as between nls and glm.)
As I said (and you can fillow up the reference), linearization and using
(n)lme *may* help.

The (prototype?) extension called GLME may be appropriate, but even
nlme relies on approximations that are not always adequate.

*Anything* can be done in S-PLUS: S is a true programming language.
But the methodology for fitting logistic mixed effects models is as far as
I am concerned an active research area.  We probably agree what we would
like to do, but finding adequate approximations is difficult, and showing
that they are adequate is harder still.

-- 
Brian D. Ripley,                  ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk
Professor of Applied Statistics,  http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~ripley/

you on the proviso that we check it using the GLIM macro.

messages.subject: Re: [S] list merging
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrea

At 09:50 AM 5/17/00 +0100, Andrea Spano wrote:
>
>I am not sure how to solve this problem
>
>l1 <- list(a=1:2, b=2:3)
>l2 <- list(a=3:4, b=4:5)
>
>and I want as a result a list l3
>
>> l3
>$a:
>[1] 1 2 3 4
>
>$b:
>[1] 2 3 4 5
>
>The resulting list should be a merge of the two lists, I know that both list
>have the same variables names (a and b).
>
>Any idea of a function that does it??

If the component sizes within each list are equal this is a data frame
operation and that's the way to do it:

l3 <- as.list(rbind(data.frame(l1), data.frame(l2)))

If they are not equal and you simply want to collect all components with
the same names in each list I would try something like

l3 <- lapply(names(l1), function(x) c(l1[[x]], l2[[x]]))
names(l3) <- names(l1)

Bill Venables

messages.subject: Re: [S] permutations
messages.body_plain:
At 06:17 AM 5/18/00 +0100, Chris Evans wrote:
>
>Has anyone written a function to produce all the permutations of n 
>(low n!) objects?  Someone has asked me to give them all the 
>perms of 5 objects for an experiment and I used to have a crude 
>Borland Basic program to do this but BB no longer runs on my 
>machine (and I'm not sure where I've put the program!) I'm buried in 
>other things and thought someone on the list must have already 
>done this though a search of my archives produced combinations 
>but not permutations.
>
>Anyone?

No but the problem is mildly fascinating.  Here is a first cut:

perm <- function(set) {
        if((n <- length(set)) <= 1)
                return(set)
        nfact1 <- prod(1:(n - 1))
        nfact <- nfact1 * n
        X <- matrix(rep(set, rep(nfact1, n)), nfact, n)
        m2 <- 0
        for(i in 1:n) {
                m1 <- m2 + 1
                m2 <- m2 + nfact1
                X[m1:m2, 2:n] <- Recall(set[ - i])
        }
        X
}

Quick check:

perm(letters[1:3])
     [,1] [,2] [,3] 
[1,] "a"  "b"  "c" 
[2,] "a"  "c"  "b" 
[3,] "b"  "a"  "c" 
[4,] "b"  "c"  "a" 
[5,] "c"  "a"  "b" 
[6,] "c"  "b"  "a" 

> perm(1:4)
      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] 
 [1,]    1    2    3    4
 [2,]    1    2    4    3
 [3,]    1    3    2    4
 ....
[23,]    4    3    1    2
[24,]    4    3    2    1
> 

Looks OK.
>

messages.subject: [S] plot.timeSeries / scaling of time-axis
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-users,

I have a very long time series (N > 30000) covering the period from
August 1996 to May this year.  The data is stored as an object created
by timeSeries().  Plotting part of the series works fine, but when I
plot the whole series I get a warning: "Points outside plot scale
moved inside in: user.to.plot(x, x.scale)".  Moreover, the plot is
clearly wrong in that some parts of the time-axis are cramped together
(verified by plotting the data using an other approach).  

Has somebody seen similar problems?
Is it a bad idea to rely on plot.timeSeries()? 
Does a solution exist?

I use S-PLUS 5.1r1 on HP-UX 10.2.

There are some details below.

Regards,
Henrik

Details:

I turns out that the warning is generated by the second last line in
plot.timeSeries() and 'plot.args' created in the third last line looks
like this:

$x.scale:
$x.scale$user.coordinates:
 [1] 08/13/1996 08/13/1996 09/27/1996 09/27/1996 03/24/1997 03/24/1997
 [7] 04/21/1997 04/21/1997 09/01/1997 09/01/1997 09/08/1997 09/08/1997
[13] 09/15/1997 09/15/1997 09/17/1997 09/17/1997 09/18/1997 09/18/1997
[19] 09/22/1997 09/22/1997 10/10/1997 10/10/1997 10/14/1997 10/14/1997
[25] 10/20/1997 10/20/1997 02/26/1998 02/26/1998 05/20/1998 05/20/1998
[31] 03/14/2000 03/15/2000

$x.scale$plot.coordinates:
 [1] 0.00000000 0.05776699 0.06776699 0.12003236 0.13003236 0.18229773
 [7] 0.19229773 0.24456311 0.25456311 0.30682848 0.31682848 0.36909385
[13] 0.37909385 0.43135922 0.44135922 0.49362460 0.50362460 0.55588997
[19] 0.56588997 0.61815534 0.62815534 0.68042071 0.69042071 0.74268608
[25] 0.75268608 0.80495146 0.81495146 0.86721683 0.87721683 0.92948220
[31] 0.93948220 1.00000000

For the first three elements the difference in user coordinates is 

    21h, 44d 5h

and in plot coordinates

To me this seems to be very wrong!  For shorther time series

messages.subject: [S] profile.ms
messages.body_plain:
I use S-PLUS 4.5 Professional on a Windows machine.  I am having trouble
using profile.ms().  I use ms() to obtain maximum likelihood estimates for
an animal mark-recapture model with Poisson errors.  I then use profile.ms()
to obtain 95% likelihood intervals.  The parameters I estimate are
probabilities and I use the logistic transformation to constrain them to (0,
1).  I have trouble with profile.ms() when parameters are at either end of
this interval.  For instance, if an estimated probability is effectively
zero (e.g., -20 on the transformed scale), changes in the transformed
parameter (e.g., from -20 to -19) cause essentially no change in the log
likelihood.  In this case, profile.ms() results in the following:

  Error in profile.ms: Missing value where logical needed:
if(abs(zeta[count]) > zetamax) break

I created my own function from profile.ms() by removing one of the while
loops - if the estimated parameter is effectively zero, I'm only interested
in the upper limit of the likelihood interval.  This new function seems to
work except when I try to change the step size.  Then the loop stops too
early.  I was able to get the loop to continue by removing a chunk of code
whose function I don't understand:

  if (z$flags[1] > 6) {
        count <- count - 1
        break
  {

Can anyone tell me what this does and if there is a cleaner way to modify
profile.ms() to work in this situation?  I would appreciate any help in
understanding this function and finding ways to make it work.

Thanks,
Paul Rasmussen

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the assistance in advance. I'm running Splus5 on a Unix
platform.

I am having a bit of difficulty declaring a glm and am seeking some
advise to point me in the right direction. The main effects model is
declared as follows:

species.glm <- glm(species ~ zone + survey + texture + frequency, family
= binomial, na.action=an.fail, data = species.logit)

The independent predictors are zone (8 levels), survey (2 levels),
texture (5 levels) and frequency (continuous). I'm trying to determine
if the probability of a species occurrence within zones and soil texture
classes is consistent between the two survey time periods.  I'm using
family=binomial, as I consider this model to be a multinomial logit.  I
have tried to use link=logit, but this is rejected. I am also using the
na.action = na.fail, because empty cells in the contingency tables do in
fact occasionally have no count data for these combinations.  I realize
the I will need to declare some interaction terms to derive the desired
model, but first I am just trying to understand how Splus interprets the
data file and the model declaration. If anyone has some suggestions I'd
really appreciate the assistance.

A very partial listing of the data set (created using read.table) is as
follows;

messages.subject: Re: [S] General linear models
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 18 May 2000, Steve Friedman wrote:

> 
> Thanks for the assistance in advance. I'm running Splus5 on a Unix
> platform.
> 
> I am having a bit of difficulty declaring a glm and am seeking some

glm = generalized linear model, not General linear models.

> advise to point me in the right direction. The main effects model is
> declared as follows:
> 
> species.glm <- glm(species ~ zone + survey + texture + frequency, family
> = binomial, na.action=an.fail, data = species.logit)

>>From the example below, species has > 2 levels. That's not how glm works.

> The independent predictors are zone (8 levels), survey (2 levels),
> texture (5 levels) and frequency (continuous). I'm trying to determine
> if the probability of a species occurrence within zones and soil texture
> classes is consistent between the two survey time periods.  I'm using
> binomial, as I consider this model to be a multinomial logit. I
> have tried to use link=logit, but this is rejected. 

Hmm, you can't do that. Either you need a surrogate Poisson model or
(better) software to fit a multiple logistic model (like multinom in the
VR bundle).

> I am also using the
> na.action = na.fail, because empty cells in the contingency tables do in
> fact occasionally have no count data for these combinations.  I realize
> the I will need to declare some interaction terms to derive the desired
> model, but first I am just trying to understand how Splus interprets the
> data file and the model declaration. If anyone has some suggestions I'd
> really appreciate the assistance.
> 
> A very partial listing of the data set (created using read.table) is as
> follows;
> 
> record survey zone texture           species    frequency
>  1      1    1       1                  Ash         2
>  2      1    1       1                Aspen        59
>  3      1    1       1           Balsam fir       183
>  4      1    1       1                Birch       251
>  5      1    1       1            Jack pine        95
>  6      1    1       1                Larch        68
>  7      1    1       1                Maple         8
>  8      1    1       1 Northern White Cedar        80
>  9      1    1       1             Red Pine         8
> 10      1    1       1               Spruce       349
> 11      1    1       1           White pine        88
> 12      1    1       2                  Ash        58
> 13      1    1       2                Aspen      1242
> 14      1    1       2           Balsam fir       834
> 15      1    1       2                Birch      1619
> 
> When Splus reads the table, how are the first three parameters defined
> (are they recognized to be factors), if not what is the most appropriate
> approach to follow to coerce them to factors?

You should do things like

df$survey <- factor(df$survey)

before any model-fitting.

What is `frequency'? It seems to be a count (not continuous), in which case
it should appear as the weights (in a multinom model) or the response
(in a surrogate Poisson model).

Try

multinom(species ~ zone + survey + texture, weights=frequency, data=df)

_or_

glm(frequency ~ zone*survey*texture + species*(zone + survey + texture),
    family=poisson, data=df)

(I could suggest looking up some examples in a good book, but S-news
is probably tired of hearing me say that.)

Are the species mutually exclusive?  If not you have coupled
binomial models for each species, and you need to fit coupled logistic
models.  You can do that via my nnet function, but it is considerably
harder.

--

messages.subject: [S] using apply to loop
messages.body_plain:
I am running SP2000 on Nt 4.0.

I am trying to generate a randomization distribution.  I thought that
the following would provide a mechanism for iterating through a complex
computation on large objects:

#############
# Encapsulate estimation computation in function
RandStat.f<- function(dummy) {
  -    RandOrder<- sample(dim(y.mtx)[1]) # y.mtx and other objects in
database at top of search path visible in f
  -    process y[RandOrder,] to get RandStat.vec
  -     assign("StatRandDist.mtx", cbind(StatRandDist.mtx, Stat.vec),
frame=0)
}

# Put actual data statistic in first column of Stat.RandDist
assign("StatRandDist.mtx", ActualDataStat.vec, frame=0)

Nrand<-1000
RandCtl<-matrix(1:Nrand,nrow=1)

set.seed(1)
apply(RandCtl,2, FUN=RandStat.f)

#######################
This seems to work - for Nrand=5, it can be used to generate  5
replicates of the statistic computed on the randomized data.  For large
Nrand the computation eventually abends with a message indicating that
the system cannot provide the required dynamic memory.  Could anyone
direct me to the relevent documentation on how frames are accumulated in
memory?  Can someone guess what I'm trying to do (like a good consultant
must do for clients) and lead me toward the path of discovery?  Thanks.

-francois

messages.subject: Re: [S] Strange results
messages.body_plain:
It's called rounding error!  You are doing arithmetic on numbers with
vastly different sizes.  Now

options(digits=16) # to see full accuracy
> exp( - d * u) * (u +1/d)
[1] 1144150319.498277
> exp( - d * v) * (v + 1/d)
[1] 1144150319.498277 1144150319.498277 1144150319.498276 1144150319.498277
[5] 1144150319.498277 1144150319.498276

The answers do differ, but really only due to rounding. Since u is 0,
you really have  exp( - d * v) * (v + 1/d) - 1/d.

> and how can i correct for it?

Re-arrange your calculations to avoid such disastrous cancellation.

(exp(-d*v) - 1)/d  is very close to -v.
exp( - d * v) * v is also very close to v.
but exp( - d * v) * v - (exp(-d*v) - 1)/d seems accurate enough.
 
Try a  series  expansion. I get

(-dv + (dv)^2 + ...)/d  + (1 - dv + ...)v  = dv^2/s - dv^2 = -dv^2/2

and you can refine this with more terms.

messages.subject: [S] A 5.1 .First funny?
messages.body_plain:
I've been experimenting a bit with Splus 5.1 (on a Sun under Solaris
2.7) --- up till now I've stuck with 3.4, although 5.1 is available
on one of the machines in our network.

In the course of fiddling around and setting things up, I seem to
have discovered something weird with the .First function.

It seems that if there are assignments in the .First function,
then these assignments take effect in the permanent data base.

To illustrate, I stripped down my .First function to:

function()
{
        foo <- "xxx"
        invisible()
}

I did an ls():

[1] ".First"      ".Last.value"

I quit from Splus, restarted, and did an ls():

[1] ".First"      ".Last.value" "foo"

The value of foo is indeed the character string "xxx":
> foo
[1] "xxx"

Has anyone else noticed this phenomenon?  Am I correct in asserting
that this is a bug?  Why is it happening?  Can I do anything about it?

                                        cheers,

                                                Rolf Turner
                                                rolf at math.unb.ca

P. S.  The permanent assignment seems ***not*** to take place if
       .First() is invoked from the command line:

> rm(foo) 
> ls()
[1] ".First"      ".Last.value"
> .First()
> ls()
[1] ".First"      ".Last.value"

I think this is ***weird***!

Dear Splus-users
I don't know how to solve this so I would very much appreciate any help that
you could kindly give me:
I want to automate the production of Box-plots:

- All my data is in the same table: Stat1995
- The x coord, which represent different scenarios (factors) for the
phenomena I want to study, is in column 15. Values in this column go from 0
to 5, each value represent a different scenario.
- The y-coord in the plots is in column 12
- Each record in my table has the provincial code in the column 1:
"Province". There is always more than 1 record with the same province code.

- Provinces do not necessarily have values in all the 6 scenarios
- There is no NA

Here is an example:
col1.....col12...col15
Prov   .. y ..   factor(x)
------------------------
I046      ...          0  ............
I046      ...          0  ..................
I046      ...          1  ..................
I046      ...          1  ...........................
I046                   1  ...........................
I054                   1 .......................
I054                   2 ........................
I054                   2 .........................
I054                   3 .....................
I054                   2 .......................
E004                  4 ...................
E004                  4
E004                  1
E004                  1
E004                  0
F030                  5
F030                  5
F030                  5
F030                  0
F030                  0

Now, I need to make these box plots by Provinces. That is: for each province
code, I want to produce a different graph (using always the same x and y
co-ordinates). The province code is also in a vector called: vect.prov.

This is what I'm trying and the error message I get:
----------------------------------------------------
> for(i in vect.prov) {
 boxplot(split(fpiStat1995[fpiStat1995[, 1] == i, 12],
fpiStat1995[fpiStat1995[, 1] == i,

different
Dumped

On the contrary, If I do it fixing the Province it works (see below), why

> boxplot(split(fpiStat1995[fpiStat1995[, 1] == "E024", 12],
fpiStat1995[fpiStat1995[, 1] ==
 "E024", 15]), main = "test")

Thank you very much
Kind regards,
Ana Sebastian

messages.subject: [S] Getting the breakpoints from cut()
messages.body_plain:
If I cut a continuous variable into N categories:

> x_runif(10)
> cut(x,3)
 [1] 1 2 2 1 3 3 3 2 3 1
attr(, "levels"):
[1] "0.02288766+ thru 0.3435332" "0.34353315+ thru 0.6641786"
[3] "0.66417865+ thru 0.9848241"

 is there a way of getting the breakpoints without having to substring
out the bits from the levels attribute? I could duplicate the algorithm
used by cut.default I suppose - the crux of which is:

breaks <- seq(r[1] - 0.01 * d, r[2] + 0.01 * d, length = breaks+1)

 (where r is the range(x) and d is normally max-min). But anyway, thats
a bit kludgy (less so than parsing the levels attribute I guess!) and 
could break easily - 0.01 seems an arbitrary bit of padding either side
of the limits.

 Any neater ideas? I've already written a levels parser...

Barry Rowlingson,
Computing Officer
Maths and Stats
Lancaster University, UK

messages.subject: Re: [S] Contrasts in lme-models
messages.body_plain:
> Date: Mon, 22 May 2000 16:08:22 +0200
> To: s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
> From: Daniel Erdin <erdin at inw.agrl.ethz.ch>
> Subject: [S] Contrasts in lme-models 
> X-loop: s-news
> 
> 
> Hello
> I'm working with Splus 4.5 on Windows NT 4.0.
> In lm-/aov-models I can test contrasts (different levels of a factor
> effect) with C(factor.name, cont) where factor.name is the name of the
> factor and "cont" is a contrast-matrix which I have to create myself. It
> seems, that I can't do exactly the same in lme-models, at least I get error
> messages. I can change the contrast type in general with
> options(contrasts=c(...)) but I would like to put specific contrasts.
> So: Can I test contrasts with lme? What am I missing?

First, as far as I recall S-PLUS 4.5 has nlme2, and I suggest you move
to nlme3, which is available from nlme.stat.wisc.edu (and a
not-quite-the-latest version is in in S-PLUS 2000.)

I don't know exactly what you are doing, not why it does not work.
As you will see later,  C() seems to work for me.
However, Let me suggest what I would have done, which is to use
the contrasts replacement function. Here's an example from MASS3

library(MASS)
library(nlme3, first=T)
oats.lme <- lme(Y ~ N + V, random = ~1 | B/V, data = oats)
summary(oats.lme)

Now, let's set contrasts:

contrasts(oats$V) <- contr.treatment(3)
contrasts(oats$N) <- contr.treatment(4)

This gives the same results as if
options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))
had been used. So does

oats.lme <- lme(Y ~ C(N,contr.treatment(4))  + C(V, contr.treatment(3)), random 
= ~1 | B/V, data = oats)
summary(oats.lme)

but the results are uglier.

The same things seem to work for nlme2, too:

oats$sp <- model.matrix(~ V - 1, oats)
oats.lme <- lme(Y ~ C(N,contr.treatment(4))  + C(V, contr.treatment(3)), 
    random = ~ sp, cluster = ~ B, 
    data = oats, re.block = list(1, 2:4),
    re.structure = c("unrestricted", "identity"),
    control = lme.control(tol=1e-10, ms.tol=1e-10)) 
summary(oats.lme)

--

> Dear all,
> 
> I am looking for a way to obtain the unique rows in a data frame; in the
> same way the function unique() returns the unique elements of a vector.
> 
> E.g. In the following data frame, there are three unique rows;
>   X   Y   Z
> 1 A   2   x
> 2 A   4   x
> 3 B   1   y
> 4 B   1   y
> 
> The unique rows are; 
>   X   Y   Z
> 1 A   2   x
> 2 A   4   x
> 3 B   1   y
> 

The usual idea is to turn it into a vector: this is used in merge, for example.

One idea is

keys <- apply(df, 1, function(x) paste(x, collapse="\r"))
df[!duplicated(keys), ]

which assumes "\r" does not appear in the data frame (very unlikely).
(merge() uses "\001", also unlikely.)  As you will see, keys is an
encoding of each row as a character string.

Brian

messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: Unique rows in a table
messages.body_plain:
> Date: Tue, 23 May 2000 15:36:51 +0000
> From: Alberto Murta <amurta at ipimar.pt>
> X-Accept-Language: en
> CC: s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
> Subject: Re: [S] Summary: Unique rows in a table
> X-loop: s-news
> 
> 
> Just a curiosity: if one uses 
> 
> > do.call("paste",frame)) 
> 
> paste joins the elements of each row, while if 
> 
> >paste(frame)
> 
> is used, the function paste joins the elements of each column. I looked
> for an explanation in help(do.call) and in John Chambers' book
> "Programming with data" but I couldn't find one.

(Well, that is not the sort of detail that book goes into: it concentrates
on design issues.)

do.call("paste",frame)

treats the data frame as a list of separate vectors, and so has several
objects as arguments.  In the original example:

> df
  X Y Z 
1 A 2 x
2 A 4 x
3 B 1 y
4 B 1 y

It is equivalent to paste(df$X, df$Y, df$Z), which gives
[1] "1 2 1" "1 4 1" "2 1 2" "2 1 2"
the numbers coming because the factor columns have been coerced to numeric
not character.

So, that isn't a valid solution in general, as you might have character
columns in the data frame and those columns might contains spaces.
As in the following contrived example

> df1 <- data.frame(A=I(c("A B", "A")), B=I(c("C", "B C")))
> df1
    A   B 
1 A B C  
2 A   B C
> do.call("paste",df1)
[1] "A B C" "A B C"
> df1[!duplicated(do.call("paste",df1)),] # wrong answer
    A B 
1 A B C

Something like

mypaste <- function(...) paste(..., sep="\001")
df1[!duplicated(do.call("mypaste",df1)),]

will work though.

--

create castor.hlp.

(which already contains _Data, _Prefs, and maybe funs and src directories).

messages.body_plain:
Dear Winnie:

>   For instance, I can
> quickly graph up a scatter plot of two continuous data types, but the
> program locks up when I try to do a pie chart on categorical data with 10
> categories. 
> 
I view this as a message from the statistical gods that one should not be
doing pie charts! ( ;-) )

Seriously, see Cleveland, W. (1994), THE ELEMENTS OF GRAPHING DATA, Hobart
Press for some good reasons why not.

As for your difficulties, I leave it to other heads wiser than I to ferret
out the source of your problems. But do note that you may need to adjust
your object.size component of options (see the options() help)  to take
advantage of the memory that you have; you can also improve data frame
handling by getting rid of the row.names of the data frames (set the
row.names equal to "" with the dup.row.names argument =T in the data.frame
constructor). But, again, these are just general comments and others might
give the exact prescription you need.

Cheers,

> Like Win, as a new S-plus user I'm astonished at how long it takes to do
> apparently simple tasks on (admittedly) large data sets -- for example, a
> histogram of 100,000 observations on one of the variables in my company
> accounts data set takes *20+ minutes, where DataDesk takes about 1/2 second.

How did you do it?  There are several ways to histograms in S, of which
histrogram() in Trellis is by far the slowest.

> I'm using a slightly less powerful set-up (only 256MB of RAM, and Windows
> 95).

Windows 95 could be called a great deal less powerful.  For a start,
can it handle the caching of more than 64Mb?  (It used not to.)

> I bought S-plus to do kernel density estimation, which I take it is a bit
> more demanding computationally than drawing a histogram. Will I be able to
> get any output in time to submit my thesis (due in 18 months or so)?

Yes, but you may have to use something less naive that density() to
do it.  Matt Wand's KernSmooth library (pre-compiled version at
http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/SWin and on statlib) is one of the best
tools, but there are others.

A quick check on a 70MHz(!) 96Mb Sparc 20, S-PLUS 3.4:

library(MASS)
x <- rnorm(1e5)
truehist(x)  # 7 secs
density(x)   # 2.2 secs
library(KernSmooth)
bkde(x, bandwidth=dpik(x)) # 4.8 secs

So a start-of-art method including bandwidth selection is a little less
than instantaneous on my 5-year-old machine.  That I manage to do so
much useful work on so lowly a machine belies rather the arguments that
S-PLUS is slow.  (Don't feel sorry for me: I can rlogin to
multiprocessor 400-650MHz machines with a Gigabyte or more, and my
laptop is pretty fast too.)

messages.subject: [S] Summary: mixed logistic model
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Renaud Lancelot, Win Lambert, Andy Cooper, Ross Darnell, and
Brian Ripley for their helpful replies to my question.  My original posting
and a summary of the responses are given below.  This list rules.

JVA

`·.,,  ><(((º>   `·.,,  ><(((º>   `·.,,  ><(((º>

Jean V. Adams
USGS - Great Lakes Science Center
1451 Green Road,  Ann Arbor, MI 48105-2807  U.S.A.
phone: (734) 214-9307,  FAX: 734-994-8780
e-mail: jean_adams at usgs.gov

Original posting:

I have some binomial data which I'd like to analyze using logistic
regression.  The catch is that I'd like to use a mixed model approach.  Is
there such a thing as mixed model logistic regression analysis?  Is there a
way to do it in S-PLUS?  Is this appropriate?

Here's a brief description of my data.  I have information on the size of
fish (length) taken from many streams (51) in several different geographics
locations (~ 10) , and I want to relate this to the probability that the
fish undergo a specific biological transformation (a binomial response,
either the fish did or did not transform).  The transformation is strongly
related to size, but the size "cutoff" at which the transformation takes
place is different for different populations (i.e., streams).  In addition
I would like to assess which model is more appropriate ... a single model
(relating length to probability of transformation) for ALL the regions or a
separate model for each region (i.e., are regional differences
significant?).  Length and region are fixed effects, and stream is a random
effect.

Summary of replies:

Renaud Lancelot:

Little hope to use S+ for this. If you're nor interested in the random
effects, and just want to correct for within-cluster correlation, you
can use GEE approach, available in yags library, on Statlib or at
http://biosun1.harvard.edu/~carey/index.ssoft.html

Basic references for GEE approach:
Liang, K.-Y., Zeger, S.L., 1986. Longitudinal data analysis using
generalized linear models. Biometrika, 73 (1): 13-22.
Zeger, S.L., Liang, K.-Y., 1986. Longitudinal data analysis for discrete
and continuous outcomes. Biometrics, 42 : 121-130.

Win Lambert:

The GUI interface is so flexible and quick with graphics I would suggest
looking at the data altogether and individually by stream.  The individual
plots should give you an idea if some streams can be lumped together in a
region.  I am essentially doing the same thing with meteorological data in
Florida.  We essentially have 2 seasons down here - warm and cool.  Within
each season, however, some months are wet and some are dry.  I'm still
analyzing, but after looking at individual plots, it looks like I can lump
December/January/February, March/April/May, etc. together and come up with
just 4 regression equations instead of 12.  Granted, 51 graphs are more of
a
pain to analyze then 12, but a visual analysis of the graphs should give
you
an idea of which belong in what region and if you can narrow it down.  I
hope this helps.

Andy Cooper:

I think SAS also has a generalized mixed-effects model (which is what
you're
looking for) called GLIMMIX.

The program R (the shareware version of Splus) has a generalized
mixed-effects model library called glmm.  The program SABRE, which is also
shareware, is specifically designed for logistic mixed-effect models
(thought it doesn't estimate BLUPs).  Unfortunately, I seem to have lost
all
my web links for these programs, but they should be pretty easy to find.

Ross Darnell:

The approach described by Murray Aitkin in Biometrics 55,167--128 uses
Gaussian quadrature. There is a GLIM macro available (see reference)
that might help with your problem.  I have a rudimentary S program
that seems to do the same thing (well it gets the same results as the
GLIM macro but is a little buggy). I would be willing to share it with
you on the proviso that we check it using the GLIM macro.

Brian Ripley:

There certainly is such a thing, and more generally GLMMs. It is not
currently easy to do in S-PLUS, and to some extent not at all due to the
integrations that are needed.

Um. Why is stream a random effect?   You are interested in the effect of
length and region, and it is usual (e.g. in anova with block designs) to
condition on incidental random effects.  Since you seem only to expecting
this to be a shift on linear predictor scale, comparing glm models

stream + length
stream + length + region
stream + length * region

ought to give valid inferences on the different fixed effects terms.
You will get some non-estimable terms if streams are nested in regions,
so a cleaner view might be

stream + length
region + stream %in% region + length
region + stream %in% region + length + region:length

and for the latter you can also fit region-specific models and sum
log-likelihoods and deviances.
There is another problem too. If streams occur within regions, and regions
are a fixed effect, streams cannot be a random effect, or at least you
will need to stratify on region.  If you want to consider random effects
you need to identify the populations from which they are drawn.

Now, if you really need random effects, I would group the data on length
groups to get binomial responses.  Then you could use lme on a linearized
version of the problem.  That is fit a binomial glm, and take out the
weights and responses from the final step of the IWLS, and use that
linearized model in lme.  (I understand that a package GLME is in the
pipeline doing this for you.)  There is an OME example in V&R3 and its
exercises doing essentially this using nlme (it is not just logistic).
The reason for grouping is that without it the linearization may well not
be adequate.  If linearized methods are not adequate, you could use MCMC
approaches, of which for this problem there are several variants.

Another approach you could consider is GEE, that will allow correlated
responses within streams. If the simple shift-in-linear-predictor model
is adequate, this seems far too complicated to specify in correlation
terms.

messages.subject: RE: [S] computing power
messages.body_plain:
I've been looking into the problem Winnie Lambert reports.  It seems to
occur with some of the table-based GUI graphs (including Pie and BarChart)
when a (not particularly) long data column is used.  I haven't been able to
reproduce any problem with histograms using the GUI as Julian Wells reported
(and as Brian Ripley kindly pointed out that the various command-line
versions are unaffected), although perhaps Julian was referring to a barplot
and not a histogram.  In any case, we're investigating now.

The command-line functions aren't affected, so an alternative is to consider
the functions pie() and barplot().  For example, using data of the
dimensions described:

## create sample data, 168000 observations, 10 categories, 6500 NAs
testdata <- factor(sample(letters[1:10],168000,replace=T))
testdata[sample(168000,6500)] <- NA

## table data in preparation for plotting
tab <- table(as.character(testdata),exclude=NULL)

## create pie chart and bar plot
pie(tab, names=names(tab),inner=1.1)
barplot(tab,names=names(tab))

Both of these plots are almost instantaneous.

# David Smith

messages.subject: [S] linux vs NT performance bottlenecks
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to make an informed choice between v5.1 for Linux and
Splus 2000 (really the choice is whether to invest in the software for
Linux since I have access to both systems).

I have two types of problems to consider:

1) Inefficient, but almost surely unavoidable, loops, of the form

  for (i in 1:lots)
    some.func(data object indexed by i, another object indexed by i)

2) Variograms and other spatial statistics with *lots* of data points

On my old system (Splus 3.4 for solaris on a sparc10), memory-hogging
processes like (1) above would take hours, but keep grinding away,
whereas on a Pentium II 233mhz, Splus 4.5 for NT, Splus just hangs.  My
assumption (perhaps naive) has been that this difference was due to
basic differences in process management between UNIX and NT.

Does anyone have observations as to how the Linux and NT versions
compare with respect to problems like those above?  All other things, such
as efficiency of code, being equal.  I'd be especially interested in
where the bottlenecks are in either/both system, i.e., CPU speed, RAM,
swap space, in case I can buy my way out of poor programming style.  :-(

If the devil is in the details, i.e., my description of the problems
would have to be more specific, that would also be useful to know.

Thanks in advance for any comments, cogent or otherwise.

messages.subject: [S] Summary Bootstrap Question
messages.body_plain:
Thanks toTim Hesterberg and Angelo Canty for responding to my post
(5/11/200) asking for help in performing block bootstrapping.   Both suggested
that I need to write my own sampling function that would accomodate sampling by
blocks within groups.   The two responses and suggested functions for doing
this:

Tim Hesterberg.

You wrote:
>       I am fitting a generalized model to daily data that extends
>over a number of years.  I want to be able to bootstrap the
>regression coefficients (and perhaps other stats) within groups
>(years) but also by blocks of say consecutive three day periods to
>preserve serial correlation known to exit.  The data looks something
>like this:
>
>   Date       Yr        Ozone         Temp           Wspd      Other variables
>   June 1     94           100             72                3.4
>........
>   June 2     94             85             88                4.3
>........
>   June 3     94             .                   .                    .
>.....
>     ........
>   Oct 30     99            120            76                4.5
>.........
>
> One form of the model being evaluated is:
>
>  Ozfit <- glm(Ozone ~ ns(temp,5) + ns(wspd,5 ) + .... + ns(yr,5),
>family=quasi(link=log),  data= ..  )
>I can bootstrap the reg coefficients nicely with
>
>  Ozfit.boot <-     bootstrap(data = ..., statistic = coef(eval(Ozfit$call)), B
>= 200, group = yr)
>
>Is there some way I can use the bootstrap function (or the boot
>function from statlib), to handle the serial correlation,
>e.g. bootsrap blocks of days so that each block of days would be
>sampled rather than each day?  Any other suggestions for handling
>this issue are welcome.  I am using Splus Pro 2000 release 2.
>Thanks.

You may pass a "sampler" of your choice to bootstrap(), including
a sampler that does block bootstrapping.
For example,

samp.boot.block <-
function(n, B, blockLength = 20)
{
  # Simple block bootstrap, overlapping blocks, no wrap-around,
  # no matching of ends.
  # To change blockLength use make.samp.boot.block()
  nblocks <- ceiling(n/blockLength)
  x <- sample(1:(n-blockLength+1), B*nblocks, replace=T)
  dim(x) <- c(nblocks, B)
  apply(x, 2, function(y, L) (0:(L-1)) + rep(y, each=L), L=blockLength)[1:n,]
}

make.samp.boot.block <- function(blockLength){
  # return a copy of samp.boot.block with the desired blockLength
  f <- samp.boot.block
  f$blockLength <- blockLength
  f
}
make.samp.boot.block(5)

samp.boot.block(5, 10, 3)
samp.boot.block(6, 10, 3)
bootstrap(1:25, mean)
bootstrap(1:25, mean, sampler=make.samp.boot.block(5)) # larger standard error

Angelo Canty

You essentially want to bootstrap a time series.  The function tsboot
(in my library from statlib) will do this.  One potential difficulty
is that you cannot specify strata (years) to this function but I am
not sure that you should be doing that in your case anyway.  If you
really want to include this then I'm afraid that you need to write
your own sampling function and use sim="parametric" in function boot.
One possible sampling function could be

blockboot.gen <- function(orig, mle) {
# mle is the block length.
    strata <- unique(orig$year)
    out <- orig
    for (s in strata) {
       dat <- orig[orig$year==s,]
       ns <- nrow(dat)
       nb <- ceiling(ns/mle)
       starts <- sample(ns-mle+1,nb,replace=T)
       inds <- apply(cbind(starts,mle-1),1,function(x)
x[1]:sum(x))[1:ns]
       out[out$year==s,] <- dat[inds,]
    }
    out
}

Note that since you are fitting a generalized linear model, you may
want to consider some form of model-based bootstrap.  You can still use
a block bootstrap as above but now just do this for some form of
residuals and add them back to the original model.  Please see chapters
7 and 8 of Davison and Hinkley (1997) for more information.

Thank to each of you.  Each suggested sampling function does the job nicely.

Bill Cox

Renaud Lancelot, F. Tussell, and Robert Key.
All suggestions don't provide some sort of regression coefficients, or rules,
with which to get fitted values at other "x" values.  I probably wasn't clear
enough on this one; the Splus function predict IS NOT AN OPTION, whatever I will
come up with will be used in a production environment on a main frame computer
in I don't even know which language, maybe SAS but that's just a guess.

Let me explain the problem.  I have a glm model fitting some tabled data.
Suppose amongst the predictors, all factors by the way, I have an "age" factor,
the levels being c("0-20", "20-30", "30-40", ... , "over 100"), say.  I got
regression estimates for all levels of that factor, the reference level having
coefficient 0.  Given we have a person 32 years old, we want to "refine" a
little bit the coefficient we got for the "30-40" group.  How can that be done.
Using the coefficients as dependent and the middle of the age brackets as
predictors I can get very good predictions at intermediate age levels using some
of the Splus smoothers, or something like «lm(y ~ ns(x), ...) but I don't get
"rules" that could be used in a different language to get estimates at
intermediate values?  I could use linear interpolation between the values at
which I get estimates, but the original curve sure doesn't seem linear.  Any

messages.subject: RE: [S] Editing labels in trellis graphs
messages.body_plain:
Speaking for my one opinion (and not for MathSoft), I actually like the GUI
graphs.  I find them useful for exploratory work, particularly when I get a
new data set and want a quick graphical look at the variables.  I'll also
generally use the GUI for Trellis graphics, which I find a lot quicker than
having to write a panel function for something beyond the basics, or having
to remember exactly how to make the shingles for continuous data.  That
said, as an old S hacker at heart if I'm doing any kind of analysis at the
command line I'll generally return to command-line graphics, both for the
convenience of not switching windows and also because I generally want to
keep a record of what I've done in the script file.

I rarely convert between command-line and GUI graphs; it's generally simpler
in the long run just to change the S code.  (This is just a personal
preference, though -- the conversion routines are actually pretty stable in
S-PLUS 2000 Release 2, and I couldn't reproduce Pierre's particular problem
in this release.)  Here's a hint for Pierre -- you can add annotations,
including text, to command-line graphs without converting to objects first,
so one solution might be to draw the barchart without the label, and add it
later using the annotation tool.

As for MathSoft's decision to devoting time and effort to the GUI ... I
wasn't around when that decision was made so I can't really comment there.
My personal opinion is that it was a good one; the GUI is, IMO, a useful
tool and better yet it's brought the S language to a range of statisticians
and data analysts who otherwise would never have seen it, and as a long-time
devotee of S that can only be a good thing.

# David

messages.body_plain:
In response to David Smith's message, a confession:

I too have been seduced by the GUI for my exploratory graphing needs. As a
(formerly) die-hard Unix hacker (since 7th Edition Unix on a PDP 11/70)  my
original opinion was the same as Bert's: what a waste of time. But, speaking
of a big time-waster, I would regularly consome large quantities of time
trying to get complicated trellis graphs, with log-scaled axes, better
fonts, legends, annotations, home-grown panel functions, etc., JUST TO WORK
from the command line. After moving from Unix to S-PLUS on a honking NT box,
I finally decided to sit down for a day or so and just try to figure out
where they (Mathsoft's S-PLUS) were coming from with respect to graphics
GUIs. It was the best investment of my time I have made in a long, long
time.

I hardly ever go back to old-style graphics now:  I have found that I can
get dynamite graphics in <10% of the time I used to spend getting the right
data into the right panel function at the right time, simultaneously
side-stepping S's quaint scoping rules. (Yes, I've thought about R, but the
GUI inteface for exploratory graphics in S-PLUS is a compelling reason for
staying put.)

So, if one of your job constraints is to get rapid, sophisticated analyses
with publication quality graphics out of your group's messy Excel
spreadsheets, the GUI will make the graphics part of that constraint
infinitely easier, and S-PLUS on NT will make the rest of the constraint
doable.

End of confession.

From: Richards, Tom 
Sent: Wednesday, May 24, 2000 4:25 PM
To: 's-news'
Subject: [S] enhanced Bubble Plots

Hello:

I am using Splus 2000 under NT 4.0.

It's possible to do bubble plots using the menus, and I'm able to vary the
symbols on plots according to levels of a variable, but I REALLY want to do
the following:

I want to plot x vs y, varying symbols by treatment group, say, square,
triangle, circle.
(This alone would be easy)
Also, I want to vary the size (area, I guess) of each symbol--no matter
which type--according to the value of another continuous variable, z.
(This alone would be a bubble plot)

I guess there would be problems with such a fugure, comparing areas of
triangles and circles, but suppose I'm only interested in comparing within
figure types, but I still want all three treatments plotted on the same set
of axes.

Is this possible in Splus?  Thanks in advance...

                                Tom Richards

messages.subject: [S] ls vs. objects
messages.body_plain:
As (also) a former UNIX diehard, I much prefer "ls" to "objects".  When I
look at the code for "ls" I see:

--> ls
function(pattern = "", pos = 1)
{
        if(pattern != "")
                stop("ls() is deprecated; patterns not allowed; use
objects()")
        objects(pos)
}

Now, this is most curious.  Why didn't MathSoft provide us with this
revision of "ls"?

ls_function(pattern = "", pos = 1)
{
        objects(pos,pattern=pattern)
}

Kevin Wright, Pioneer Hi-Bred Int'l, x4054.

messages.subject: [S] spatial.cor, binary
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus,

A colleague has a question about the computation of a 2-outcome spatial autocorrelation index using the spatial.cor function in S+ Spatial stats. At present it appears the binary option has been withdrawn, leaving only the Moran's i and Geary's c options available. Neither of these options appear to be suited to binary outcome data. If you have experience with this function or know how implement it with binary outcome data could you email him directly?:

Brendan Wintle

b.wintle1 at pgrad.unimelb.edu.au

(we work with S+ v4.5 on Win NT or Win 95, and Spatial Stats v1.1)

Here is his request:

I've been trying to compute the spatial correlation index for binary

(presence/absence) data using the spatial.cor function in spatial  stats.

The manual I have (v1, 1996) tells me that I can use the option;

statistic="binary"(pg D-71).  When I use this option (on v1.1 1999), it

returns Error; 'statistic "binary" not implemented in this version'.  

Can you please tell me why this option was withdrawn? If I use the

'statistic="moran" option on a binary outcome set in spatial stats, is the

computed result equivalent to the binary measure of spatial  association?

If not, do I have any other options for computing Moran's (1948)

two-outcome measure of spatial association. 

Here is part of an answer from Mathsoft:

>>>>

> I found an existing bug report saying that the "spatial.cor()" function
>
> does not do statistic="binary".  I also found the following discussion in
>
> our database about "binary" option for "spatial.cor()" function:
>
> -------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> QUESTION:
>
> > Is there anything in S-PLUS for modelling binary spatial data, or is
>
> > there planned to be?
>
>
>
> ANSWER:
>
> > I discovered that the binary statistic for spatial.cor was not  correct
>
> > just before we released SpatialStats.
>
> >
>
> > We intend to put the binary statistic back into spatial.cor for the
>
> > next release of S+SpatialStats (no set date for that yet).
>
> -------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
>
>
> I checked the newest version of S+SpatialStats here and see that we
>
> haven't put the "binary" statistic back into "spatial.cor()" function yet.
>
> Thus, according to the above, we currently do not have any options that
>
> deal with binary spatial data.
<<<<

We appreaciate any help,

Jane Elith

messages.subject: Re: [S] ls vs. objects
messages.body_plain:
>>>>> "KWri" == Wright, Kevin <WRIGHTKEVI at phibred.com> writes:

    KWri> As (also) a former UNIX diehard, I much prefer "ls" to "objects".  
When I
    KWri> look at the code for "ls" I see:

    --> ls
    KWri> function(pattern = "", pos = 1)
    KWri> {
    KWri>  if(pattern != "")
    KWri>       stop("ls() is deprecated; patterns not allowed; use objects()")
    KWri>  objects(pos)
    KWri> }

    KWri> Now, this is most curious.  Why didn't MathSoft provide us with this
    KWri> revision of "ls"?

    KWri> ls_function(pattern = "", pos = 1)
    KWri> {
    KWri>  objects(pos,pattern=pattern)
    KWri> }

because "pattern" in ls() and objects() have very different meaning:
 "pattern" for ls         means "wildcards"
 "pattern" for objects()  means "regular expressions" [aka "regex(p)"s].
                          {the documentation ?objects mentions ?grep
                           and grep mentions reg.exp.s}

BTW:  In R  {www.r-project.org},  
      ls & objects are synonymous  {and pattern always means "regexp"}.

messages.body_plain:
At 5/24/00 at 03:53 PM, you wrote:

> I am in the market for a new machine.  Is there any advantage to S+ in
> having dual CPUs in Windows 2000 or NT?

I have been using dual-processor machines for Windows NT, and before that 
OS/2, for about 4 years now.  I find that they are worth it.  Very little, 
if any, software takes advantage of the second processor 
directly.  However, if you need to do other work while a long job in S+ is 
running, having the extra processor is extremely convenient in giving far 
better response time.  Also, one can run two long jobs simultaneously, and 
each effectively uses one processor, giving close to twice the throughput.

...MHP

messages.subject: [S] Rand and Cohen's kappa
messages.body_plain:
Dear Sir,

On the WEB I read a mail from you in which I read the following:

>What you are trying to do is the general problem of comparing partitions 
>between cluster solutions. Although people often use
>simple missclassification rates or Cohen's kappa, the best approach is to use 
>the adjusted Rand statistic which has been developed to
>do exactly what you want. For more information on the adjusted Rand, you 
>should 
>refer to Hubert, L., & Arabie, P. (1985).
>Comparing partitions. Journal of Classification, 2, 193-218.

>The Rand statistic is not available in S-Plus, or any other stats package as 
>far as I know. As luck would have it (!), I just developed
>an S-Plus function to calculate it. This is my first attempt at programming 
>with S-Plus, so I'm sure it's not the most elegant
>approach. It does get you the right answer, however!

I would like to ask you something about this. What is the reason why you prefer 
the Rand index to Cohen's kappa? Furthermore: on what scale or de adjusted Rand 
values given? Is the maximum 1 (best case) and the mininum 0 (worse case)? 
Sometimes I get negative values? Is that possible? I read the article of Hubert 
and Arabie, but it becomes not clear to me.

Sincerely yours,

Wilbert Heeringa
State University of Groningen (NL)
Alfa-Informatica

messages.subject: [S] import from Excel again!
messages.body_plain:
Truncation of fields to 32 characters without warning
is alive and well.

If the NameRow= option is used in the import.data command
with FileType="EXCEL" then truncation occurs.  The workaround
is to drop the "NameRow=" from the command.

Thanks to D. Smith of statsci for quickly verifying this so
that I could proceed to do for a fourth time what I have already
done three times. :(

I wish that statsci would post a list of known bugs so
that I could consult it from time to time to see whether
I have any problems.  It is deplorable that statsci has
such information (existence of bugs) and chooses not
to make this information available to users.

Had such a facility been in oexistence, I would have
checked it before using import.data for the first
time, and perhaps  and perhaps I would not
have incurred such a monumental and needless
waste of time.

Regards,

Bruce

********************* SCRIPT FILE ******************************

import.data("marrev.dat","c:\\data\\bia\\radmar00\\marrev.xls",FileType="EXCEL",NameRow=1,StringsAsFactors="Never")
marrev1.dat <- 
read.table("c:\\data\\bia\\radmar00\\marrev.csv",sep=",",header=T,row.names=NULL,as.is=T)

marrev.dat$market[113]
marrev1.dat$market[113]

***********************OUTPUT****************************************
> import.data("marrev.dat", 
        "c:\\data\\bia\\radmar00\\marrev.xls", FileType
         = "EXCEL", NameRow = 1, StringsAsFactors = 
        "Never")
> marrev1.dat <- read.table(
        "c:\\data\\bia\\radmar00\\marrev.csv", sep = 
        ",", header = T, row.names = NULL, as.is = T)
> marrev.dat$market[113]
[1] "Greensboro-Winston Salem-High P"
> marrev1.dat$market[113]
[1] "Greensboro-Winston Salem-High Point"

================WORK-AROUND=====================

remove "NameRow=1" from the import.data command

messages.subject: Re: [S] import from Excel again!
messages.body_plain:
I once made a solemn vow that I would NEVER post to S-News, but.....  Since
I work in a heterogeneous computing environment, I am continually shipping
data back and forth between applications and operating platforms.  I have
learned from trusty coworkers that there are many problems interacting with
Excel when text fields are concerned.  For instance, when I need to import
Excel data into SAS on a Unix box, I am safer converting the .xls to a .csv
file, not a .txt file because Excel itself truncates text fields to 32
characters in the conversion.  Other  stat software lists also have
frequent reports of problems with Excel.  Another example involves
importing text in Excel that is formatted as "General".  Good luck on that
one.  Also, when you import into Excel, Excel itself makes odd decisions
about fields, based on the contents of the first couple of rows of your
data.  I don't presume to be an expert on these issues, just admitting to
having been burned.  My conclusion: Eternal vigilance and not jumping to
conclusions about which end of a two-way communication is at fault are
required  here in the trenches.

I have a question and hope that anyone can provide me an
idea for it.

There are inputs (Insulin injection) and responses (Glucose
measures) over a period of time. They do have a strong
positive correlation, however the output measures badly
oscillates. The objective is whether we can automate the
input system by utilising the recent response measures, in
order to maintain a certain level of Glucose.

The output measures are taken every one minutes and
currently the next injection of Insulin (Input) is
determined manually by human based on the recent output
measures.

Would anyone tell me kindly what statistical procedures will
be suitable to resolve this problem?
The preferable procedures are ones not based on any
physiological models.

Many thanks in advance,
In-Sun

messages.subject: RE: [S] dates of creating an object
messages.body_plain:
Al-

Here's some related ideas that might be useful....

(1) If you are using S-Plus 2000 for Windows, then you have an Object
Browser. You can have the right pane show dates, and then click on the date
heading to sort on that. I use this all the time. Most recent objects will
be on the bottom. The left pane will show the objects sorted by name even if
they are sorted in the right pane by date, which is handy.

(2) I also bundle stuff into lists as a sort of archive when I finish a
phase of my analysis. I reserve the name r, for instance, for results. Stuff
can be added to the end like this....
r[["This is the second regression"]] _ reg.rslts
r[["This is the anova test result for the second regression"]] _ ....

I also reserve f for function calls, with similarly descriptive names. Note
that the names are not legal S-Plus names (at least they cannot be used
without quotation marks), but I don't care. I type names(r) and then extract
the list element I want later by index number, so the names merely need to
be descriptive.

(3) I use scripts a lot. These can collect all the useful commands (minus
mistakes and wrong paths) together, so it is easy to redo or slightly modify
an analysis done before.

(4) With the first three strategies, I don't save a lot of objects, because
they are easy to recreate. I reserve names beginning with a period as "junk"
variables which can be deleted after any session without harm. This
disciplines me to save vital objects under different (and more descriptive,
if longer) names at the end of a session. It also lets me use short names
that are easy to type during a work session, and as long as they start with
a period, I needn't worry that they will replace a vital object of the same
name that I created in some earlier session.

Cheers,

Terry Elrod

messages.subject: re: [S] using apply to loop
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Sam Buttrie for solving this problem.

I was using the following to accumulate randomization replicates:
>>>
# Put actual data statistic in first column of Stat.RandDist
assign("StatRandDist.mtx", ActualDataStat.vec, frame=0)
set.seed(1)
apply(1:Nrand,1, FUN=RandStat.f)

where

RandStat.f<- function(dummy) {
      RandOrder<- sample(dim(y.mtx)[1])
     { process y[RandOrder,] to get RandStat.vec}
     assign("StatRandDist.mtx", cbind(StatRandDist.mtx, RandStat.vec),
frame=0)
}
<<<

For large Nrand, I would ruin out of memory.  Sam pointed out the
problem and suggected a solutions.  I thought I was gaining something by
passing the function results through an object in frame 0.  I don't
think this achieved anything and if I ever forgot to retrieve the saved
object before q()ing, it was gone.  You only lose an object that was
constructed in an overnight job once.  After this occured, I implemented
Sam's solution and it works.

Sam's message:
>>>>>>>>>
One thing that's probably hurting you is cbind-ing every time through
the
loop. It's much more efficient to allocate the memory for your results
once;
when you cbind every time, S-Plus has to allocate memory for one column;

then it abandons that and allocates a separate piece of memory for two
columns; then for three, and so on.

Try something like this:

sams.rand.stat.f <- function(thing) {
return (francois.process (y, order = sample (nrow(y.mtx)))) #the result
of francois.process is RandStat.vec above
}

Assume that the "rand stat" thing is a vector of length n.

sapply (1:100, sams.rand.stat) will produce a n x 100 matrix without the

cbinding and I'm pretty sure it will help.

<<<<<<<<<<
It does seem to help.  Thanks.
-francois.

On Fri, 26 May 2000, Martin H. H. Stevens wrote:

> 
> I am afraid this may turn out to be an elementary statistics lesson, but
> here goes, and thanks (and/or apologies) in advance...
> 
> When I use Type I sums of squares in a linear model, the sum of squares
> of each factor (from summary.aov()) plus the residual add up to the
> total sum of squares ([n-1]*s^2 of the response variable.  When I use
> Type III SS,  I get something less than the total sums of squares when I
> add up the partial Sums of Squares....  Why?

I think the question is why you expect it to add up?

You can do analysis of variance when terms are added sequentially, and
so each term is given the reduction in SSq *after adding all the previous
terms&.  Theorem: the SSqs add up.  (Note: it is theorem, but it has
conditions.)

Now the egregious so-called type III is not an analysis of variance. Here
it is equivalent to drop1: that is it computes the increase in SSq on
dropping each term independently.  Since F1 was the last to be added, it
has the same value on dropping.  However, your first table has the SSq for
y1 alone, and the second for y1 after adding f1.

I think ssType=3 is best left to those who have been forceably
dragged away from a 3-letter statistics package which is stuck in the days
of capital letters on punched cards.  The rest of us can use drop1,
which at least does sensible things in the presence of interactions
(unless abused).

> 
> > y2 <- y1 + 50*runif(50)
> > y1 <- 1:50
> > F1 <- as.factor(c(rep("A",25),rep("B",25)))
